usage: Apply as a soil-surface drench or late-afternoon/evening foliar spray against mobile surface pests and shore flies; keep media moist and shield from UV.

origin: Occurs worldwide in greenhouses and outdoor crops.
crops: Cucumber, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Grapes, Berries, Strawberry, Apple, Hop, Fruit trees, Ornamentals
effects: Pierces and sucks cell contents on the underside of leaves. Disperses by walking or dropping to the ground when heavily infested, migrating along crop wires ('rope-down'), wind dispersal on silk threads, or mechanical/plant movement.
targets: Controlled by Phytoseiulus persimilis (SPIDEX), Neoseiulus californicus (SPICAL), Neoseiulus fallacis, Amblyseius andersoni, Galendromus occidentalis, Mesoseiulus longipes, Anystis baccarum, Stethorus punctillum, Feltiella acarisuga (SPIDEND), Macrolophus pygmaeus (MIRICAL-N), Dicyphus hesperus, and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Small, eight-legged arachnids. Adult females are about 0.5 mm long with an oval, rear-rounded body; males are smaller, narrower, and more active. Highly variable body color ranging from orange, light yellow, light green, dark green, red, brown, to almost black, heavily influenced by the host crop (e.g., yellow-brown on cucumbers, red-brown on tomatoes). Both males and females usually feature two large black spots on the body and red eyes visible across all stages.
lifeCycle: Consists of five developmental stages: egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult (with alternating active and resting periods where they do not move or feed). Females can lay more than 10 eggs per day.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Laid on leaf undersides; at 25°C, the egg stage lasts ~4.3 days.
stageBreakdown.Larva, Protonymph, Deutonymph: At 25°C, larval stage takes ~1.8 days, protonymph ~1.5 days, and deutonymph ~2.0 days, with alternating active feeding and resting periods.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females ~0.5 mm long, oval body rounded at rear; males smaller, narrower, more active. Two large black spots on body and red eyes in all stages.

conditions: Thrives best under warm and dry conditions with extremely rapid population growth and high temperature dependence (temperature limits range between 12°C and 40°C). At 25°C, generation time drops to less than two weeks (~9.6 days egg-to-adult), with populations doubling in fewer than 3 days and increasing tenfold in about 10 days under greenhouse conditions.

devTable.caption: Developmental Breakdown & Population Metrics at 25°C

damage: Piercing and sucking cell contents on the underside of leaves causes destruction of cells, leading to small yellow dots (stippling), increased transpiration, and reduced photosynthesis. Severe damage turns whole leaves yellow, and heavy infestations can completely cover plants with webs, stunting growth or causing plant death. Shows distinct stippling/damage patterns on crops like cucumbers and tomatoes.
usage: Overwintering: In temperate regions, declining day length and falling temperatures trigger diapause. Fertilized females turn orange-red and enter a dormant condition in concealed spaces or greenhouse structures, where they do not feed or lay eggs and have lower pesticide susceptibility. They resume egg-laying when conditions become favorable in spring.

synonyms: Brevipalpus californicus, Brevipalpus obovatus, Red and black flat mite
origin: Worldwide distribution found on many cultivated plants (especially a problem for greenhouse ornamentals). Raoiella indica invaded the Americas causing damage to palms, bananas, and ornamentals. Note: B. phoenicis was recently discovered to be a complex of six species.
crops: Phalaenopsis, Palms, Schefflera, Ornamentals, Citrus, Papaya, Pomegranate, Banana
effects: Moves slowly and is mostly found along the veins on the underside of leaves. Unlike true spider mites, false spider mites DO NOT produce webs. Secrete toxic saliva while feeding and several Brevipalpus species transmit plant viruses.
targets: Controlled on greenhouse ornamentals with Amblyseius swirskii (SWIRSKI-MITE / ULTI-MITE SWIRSKI) with good results in Phalaenopsis, palms, and Schefflera sp.
appearance: Brick-red to yellow in colour; smaller than true spider mites (around 0.25–0.3 mm in length). Different species look very similar. Flattened and egg-shaped when seen from above, earning them the name 'flat mites'. Their dorsal surface shows a net-like pattern, and their legs appear crumpled.
lifeCycle: Passes through the same developmental stages as true spider mites: egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Reproduction is mostly parthenogenetic (females producing almost exclusively female progeny). Adults live for about 30 days and lay around 30 eggs.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Clear red colour and elliptical; usually laid in folds in the leaf or along the mid-vein, often in dense clusters by different females.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Pass through six-legged larva and eight-legged protonymph and deutonymph stages; move slowly along leaf underside veins.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 0.25–0.3 mm long, brick-red to yellow, flattened and egg-shaped with a net-like dorsal pattern and crumpled-looking legs.

conditions: Development rate is much slower than true spider mites and depends on temperature, relative humidity, and host plant. Egg-to-adult development of B. phoenicis takes around 30–50 days at 20–21°C and about 20–25 days at 25–26°C.
damage: No webbing produced. Usually found on the underside of leaves, causing a brown, scabby discolouration spreading from both sides of the main vein into the leaf blade, leading to premature leaf aging and leaf drop. Some crops become misshapen due to toxic saliva secreted while feeding; sunken patches occur where mites feed. B. phoenicis also feeds on citrus, papaya, and pomegranate fruit.
usage: Dispersal: Short-distance dispersal by walking and long-range dispersal by wind are very limited. Main spread occurs via human handling/workers in the crop and distribution of infested plants.

synonyms: Vasates lycopersici, Vasates destructor, Phyllocoptes destructor
origin: Detected for the first time in Australia; now a pest in tomatoes in all areas where they are grown globally.
crops: Tomato, Solanaceous crops, Aubergine
effects: Does not produce galls; lives freely (vagrant) on tomato plants and feeds by sucking out the contents of epidermal plant cells. Damage starts on the lower part of the plant and moves upwards as mites ascend.
targets: No known biological control works successfully in greenhouses because tomato glandular hairs impair predatory mites (A. swirskii, A. limonicus), release sticky/toxic substances, and provide a 'forest' for russet mites to hide in.
appearance: Extremely small mites: adults are roughly 0.17 mm in length (males slightly smaller at ~0.15 mm). Elongated (torpedo-shaped), soft, and segmented. Body appears divided into two parts: the head with mouthparts, and the rest of the body. Unlike other mite groups that have four pairs of legs, ALL mobile stages of A. lycopersici have only two pairs of legs.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, first instar nymph (sometimes called larva), second instar nymph, and adult. All life stages look very similar; adults develop about 2–3 days after the second stage within a day. Fertilized eggs give rise to both males and females, whereas unfertilized eggs produce only males. A female can lay up to 3.5 eggs per day and 50 eggs in total.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Approximately 0.05 mm in diameter; transparent white to cream-yellow, wedge-shaped. Laid on the underside of leaves, on leaf petioles, and on stems, usually in the lower portion of plants.
stageBreakdown.1st & 2nd Instar Nymphs: Look very similar to adults with only 2 pairs of legs; develop rapidly (0.4 to 3.1 days combined depending on temperature).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 0.17 mm long (males 0.15 mm), torpedo-shaped, segmented, only 2 pairs of legs.

conditions: Optimal temperature for population growth is around 27°C; higher temperatures decrease oviposition and juvenile survival. Damage is most rapid at high temperatures and in hot, dry greenhouse bays where affected leaves dry out quickly.

damage: Affected leaves are slightly curled and acquire a silvery sheen on the underside, later becoming brown and brittle. Damaged leaves and stems lose their trichomes (leaf hairs). Affected stems turn a rusty-brown colour, and in serious cases may snap. If fruit is affected, the skin becomes coarse and turns reddish-brown, and the fruit itself can become deformed with surface cracking.
usage: Dispersal: Spreads through a crop mainly on air currents. When plants die, mites congregate on the highest parts of the plant where wind picks them up more easily. Also walks plant-to-plant where leaves touch or spreads on worker clothing and materials.

origin: Occurs in the tropics and in greenhouses in temperate regions worldwide.
crops: Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Tomato, Cucumber, Azalea, Begonia, Gerbera, Cyclamen, Ornamentals
effects: Found mostly on the undersides of young, expanding leaves, growing tips, flower buds, and near leaf stalks (lower leaves often remain unaffected). Toxic saliva causes malformation and distortion of above-ground growth resembling virus damage.
targets: Controlled by predatory mites Neoseiulus cucumeris (THRIPEX), Amblyseius swirskii (SWIRSKI-MITE), Neoseiulus californicus (SPICAL), Amblyseius andersoni, Amblydromalus limonicus, Transeius montdorensis, and Neoseiulus fallacis if released early in the cropping cycle.
appearance: Tarsonemidae mites have no eyes. Emerging adult is roughly 0.2 mm long, oval, broad, and pale yellow or yellow-green depending on food consumed. Females feature a distinctive white stripe on their backs. Males are smaller (~0.15 mm), taper towards the rear end, have long legs, and share the female's color but lack the white stripe.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva (3 pairs of legs), quiescent nymph (pharate female), and adult (4 pairs of legs). The last pair of legs in both males and females is reduced and not used for walking. Males use their fourth pair of legs to carry around young pharate females (quiescent nymphs) still in their larval cuticle, and mating occurs as soon as the adult female emerges. Fertilized eggs produce females; unfertilized produce males (sex ratio is 75% females). Females mate once; total eggs laid range from 15 to 50 (>4 eggs/day for young females).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Large (about 0.07 mm), elongated, and oval; transparent and speckled with longitudinal rows of white dots (tufts). Strongly attached to the surface, deposited separately in well-hidden, damp, and shady places on leaf undersides or fruit.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Quiescent Nymph: Larvae have 3 pairs of legs. Pharate females enter a quiescent nymph stage inside the larval cuticle and are carried around by adult males using their modified 4th pair of legs.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females ~0.2 mm long, oval, pale yellow/green with a white dorsal stripe; males ~0.15 mm without stripe.

conditions: Requires high relative humidity (70–90% RH, optimal 90%) and warm conditions. Activity and reproduction decline at lower temperatures. Unable to overwinter outdoors or tolerate cold conditions in temperate climates (does not enter diapause).

devTable.caption: Development (on Azalea) & Oviposition/Longevity (on Grape)

damage: Symptoms look similar to virus damage or hormonal herbicide injury. Creates brown edges at the base of young leaves, curling, bronzing, shiny leaf undersides, fine networks of brown stripes/collapsed spots, or dense corky patches where main veins stand out as a green pattern against brown leaf tissue. Severe attacks kill growing tips, halt plant growth, cause fruit deformation/corky patches/cracking, discolor flowers, and can kill the whole plant at relatively low mite populations.
usage: Dispersal & Management: Attacks are localized and spread outward gradually. Phoresy: attaches to legs of whiteflies and aphids for long-distance dispersal; also spread by workers or wind. Cultural control: remove affected plants/parts and lower relative humidity.

origin: Widespread pest in temperate climates and heated greenhouses.
crops: Strawberry, Cyclamen, Gerbera, Fuchsia, Hedera, Ornamentals
effects: Feeds on plant sap in developing tissue by penetrating plant tissue with piercing-sucking mouthparts. Avoids light and inhabits young folded leaves, flower buds, and growing shoots/crowns where humidity is highest and protected from direct sunlight (rarely on older, unfurled leaves).
targets: Controlled by predatory mites Neoseiulus californicus (SPICAL), Neoseiulus cucumeris (THRIPEX), Amblyseius swirskii, Amblyseius andersoni, and Neoseiulus fallacis, especially in strawberries.
appearance: Adult females are translucent yellowish-brown, about 0.25 mm long. In adult females, the hind legs (4th pair) are reduced to slender threadlike structures not used for walking. Males are smaller than females, and their hind legs are modified to transport pharate females.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, quiescent nymph (pharate female / false pupa), and adult. Facultative parthenogenetic: both unmated and mated females can produce male and female progeny. Females can live up to 45 days and lay 25–30 eggs.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: About half the size of the adult mite (~0.12 mm), oval, smooth, transparent, and twice as long as wide with both ends equally rounded.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Pharate Female: Larvae are opaque white with only 3 pairs of legs. Pharate females remain in their larval skin before emerging (transitional stage often called pupa, false pupa, or quiescent nymph) and are carried by males.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Yellowish-brown, ~0.25 mm long; females have threadlike 4th legs.

conditions: Under favourable conditions (20–25°C and high relative humidity of 90–100%), egg-to-adult development takes 9–12 days. At 10°C, cyclamen mites do not develop into adults in the laboratory. Adult females can overwinter outdoors in temperate areas in the crown of the plant between folded leaves or buds.

devTable.caption: Development & Oviposition on Strawberry (at 90–100% RH)

damage: Damage occurs in localized patches because the mite spreads very slowly; symptoms resemble virus damage. Infested leaves are twisted or curled, distorted, brittle, and smaller than normal. In cyclamen, flowers are damaged and leaf growth is inhibited; in Hedera, it causes stem baldness; in gerbera, flowers are deformed/discoloured and leaves turn bronze along the midrib. Damaged strawberry leaves are wrinkled/folded with unnaturally dense appearance due to short petioles; severely attacked leaves turn brown/silvery and die, and flowers/young fruits become brown near the base.
usage: Dispersal: Short-distance dispersal occurs by walking plant-to-plant; longer distances occur via air currents or human activity. If conditions become dry, mites migrate to the base/crown of the host plant and return when conditions improve.

synonyms: Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci, Echinothrips americanus
origin: Over 6,000 known species globally; fewer than 20 species cause problems in agriculture and horticulture. All greenhouse pest species belong to the family Thripidae.
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Tomato, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Impatiens, Ornamentals
effects: Pierce surface tissue cells and suck out contents, causing surrounding tissue to die. Vector dangerous plant tospoviruses, notably Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) and Impatiens Necrotic Spot Virus (INSV).
targets: Controlled by Phytoseiid mites (A. swirskii, N. cucumeris, A. limonicus, T. montdorensis, Iphiseius degenerans, Amblyseius andersoni - target larvae), Anystis baccarum, Orius predatory bugs (O. insidiosus, O. laevigatus, O. majusculus, O. strigicollis - target larvae & adults), Dicyphus hesperus, Nabis americoferus, soil predatory mites (S. scimitus, G. gillespiei, M. robustulus - target pupae), Dalotia coriaria rove beetle, and Steinernema feltiae nematodes (target pupae).
appearance: Small insects (0.5–14 mm; in temperate regions no larger than 2.5 mm) with characteristic fringed wings (eyelash-like fringe of hairs along both edges of thin wings). Species identification based on form, color, and hair pattern is only possible at the adult stage.
lifeCycle: Develops through six stages: egg, two larval instars, pre-pupa, pupal instar, and adult insect. Reproduction can be sexual or asexual: unfertilized females produce male offspring (arrhenotoky), while fertilized females produce both males and females. In species where males are rare (e.g., Thrips tabaci), females are produced parthenogenetically from unfertilized eggs.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Kidney-shaped with a white or yellow shell. Deposited inside plant tissue (leaves, flower petals, soft stalks) via the female's toothed ovipositor. On sweet pepper leaves, egg sites form recognizable wart-like growths.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (L1 & L2): Feed on all aerial parts of the plant on leaf undersides, flowers, and buds; fairly mobile, smaller than adults, and lack wings.
stageBreakdown.Pre-pupae & Pupae: Pupate on the plant (e.g., E. americanus) or in the ground/substrate (e.g., F. occidentalis, T. tabaci). Recognized by developing wing buds (pupae have longer wing buds and antennae curved back over the head). Do not feed and only move if disturbed.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Both pairs of feathered wings fully developed.

conditions: Infestations begin via plant material, adults flying in from outside, or overwintering in greenhouse crevices/fissures. (Historical note: when crops were grown in soil, soil sterilization killed many overwintering thrips; artificial substrates now allow thrips to overwinter more easily and attack young plants early). First detections typically occur near entrances, main paths, or warm spots (walls, heating pipes).
damage: Resulting silver-grey patches on leaves and black dots of excreta (frass) indicate presence. Empty cells desiccate and adjacent cells turn brown. Plant vigor drops due to chlorophyll loss; serious infestations cause leaves to shrivel, deformed flowers, and scarred fruit.
usage: Spread is active (flight) and/or passive (floating on air currents, movement of plants, materials, and humans).

origin: Originates from the West Coast of North America; spread almost worldwide over the last 30+ years. Most damaging and troublesome thrips species in greenhouse cultivation globally.
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Rose, Orchids, Ornamentals
effects: Pierces surface tissue cells and sucks out contents. Prefers hidden habitats (growing tips, flower buds, and open flowers containing pollen) and exhibits high resistance to chemical pesticides.
targets: Primary vector of Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) and Impatiens Necrotic Spot Virus (INSV). Controlled by Amblyseius swirskii, Amblydromalus limonicus, Transeius montdorensis, Neoseiulus cucumeris, Iphiseius degenerans, Amblyseius andersoni, Anystis baccarum, Orius spp., Dicyphus hesperus, Nabis americoferus, Stratiolaelaps scimitus, Gaeolaelaps gillespiei, Macrocheles robustulus, Dalotia coriaria, and Steinernema feltiae.
appearance: Adult females are 1.3–1.4 mm long and highly variable in color (ranging from almost white, yellowish-orange, to almost black; winter populations are darker than summer populations). Female abdomens narrow to a point with a clearly visible ovipositor. Males are pale, smaller than females (0.9–1.1 mm), with two visible orange patches on the abdomen. Both sexes have fully developed feathered wings.
lifeCycle: Follows the 6 stages of Thripidae: egg, two larval instars, pre-pupa, pupa, and adult. Unfertilized females produce only male progeny; fertilized females produce 70% females and 30% males. On cucumber at 25°C, females lay ~3 eggs/day, allowing populations to double in ~4 days. Pollen access drastically accelerates development and egg production.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Very small (~0.2 mm long), kidney-shaped, white-yellow; inserted into plant tissue (leaves, flower petals, soft stem parts). On sweet pepper leaves, egg-laying spots form recognizable wart-like growths.
stageBreakdown.Larva 1 & Larva 2: Young L1 larvae are 0.4–0.6 mm long, almost transparent white, yellowish, or orange-yellow with a large head and bright red eyes. Second instar (L2) larvae are 0.7–0.9 mm long.
stageBreakdown.Pre-pupae & Pupae: Usually pupates in the ground (in damp places or natural crevices up to ~15 mm beneath the surface), though pupae can also be found on leaves, flowers, or sheltered spots. Feature developing wing buds, do not feed, and only move if disturbed.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females 1.3–1.4 mm (white/yellow-orange/dark brown); males 0.9–1.1 mm (pale with 2 orange abdominal patches).

conditions: Development ceases above 35°C and below 10°C. On chrysanthemum, egg-to-adult development takes ~9 days at 30°C compared to ~40 days at 15°C. Does not enter diapause, remaining active as long as temperatures are sufficiently high; adult females seek sheltered spots to overwinter when temperatures drop.

rows: Development ceases; adults overwinter in sheltered spots
~13 days (~3 eggs/female/day on cucumber; population doubles in ~4 days)

damage: Silver-grey patches on leaves with black frass dots, chlorophyll loss, and shriveled leaves. Feeding on growing tips and flower buds causes severely deformed leaves, discolored/scarred petals, or unopened buds. Fruit damage occurs even at low densities, causing severe deformations such as 'pig-tail' fruit in cucumbers. Vector of TSWV and INSV (which often infect the same host plant concurrently).
usage: Distribution in crop: Primarily found in uppermost plant parts. On soft-leaved plants (gerbera, chrysanthemum) found on lower and upper leaf surfaces; on tougher-leaved plants (roses, orchids) prefers growing tips. Migrates to flower buds as soon as they form. Becomes active and leaves hiding places in early morning hours.

origin: Probably originates from the Middle East and countries bordering the Black and Caspian Seas; now distributed worldwide. Was the major greenhouse thrips pest until the 1980s before being largely displaced by Frankliniella occidentalis.
crops: Cucumber, Cucurbits, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Rose, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Carnation, Bulbs
effects: Pierces surface cells mainly along the main leaf veins, with most damage evident where veins join. Colonizes all plant parts, preferring the underside of young leaves in the top of the plant, but also found on shoots and flowers.
targets: Vector of Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) in some regions. Easier to control than F. occidentalis using predatory mites (A. swirskii, N. cucumeris, A. limonicus, T. montdorensis, Iphiseius degenerans) and Orius spp. (O. insidiosus, O. laevigatus, O. majusculus), plus soil predators (Stratiolaelaps scimitus, Gaeolaelaps gillespiei, Dalotia coriaria).
appearance: Adult color depends on food source: females are greyish-yellow to brown and 0.8–1.2 mm long. Males are rare, wingless, smaller, and lighter in color than females.
lifeCycle: Populations contain very few males; reproduction is generally parthenogenetic (thelytokous), with unfertilized females producing female progeny. At 25°C, a female lays 2 to 5 eggs per day and >100 eggs in total. Pupation takes place in the soil.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Similar to F. occidentalis eggs (~0.2 mm, kidney-shaped) and laid in leaf tissue.
stageBreakdown.Larva 1 & Larva 2: First instar larvae are 0.4–0.6 mm long, light in color, with a large head and bright red eyes. Second instar larvae are slightly larger and light yellow to yellowish-green.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: Pupation takes place in the soil.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females 0.8–1.2 mm, greyish-yellow to brown; males rare and wingless.

conditions: Egg-to-adult development takes ~40 days at 15°C, decreasing to 11 days at 30°C. Does not enter true diapause, but adult females survive winter in reproductive quiescence, resuming reproduction when temperatures rise.
damage: Silver-grey scarring patches concentrated along main leaf veins and vein junctions. Fruit damage (e.g., in cucumber) only occurs if the crop is heavily infested. Vector of TSWV.
usage: Monitor undersides of young upper leaves along main veins.

origin: Originates from Eastern North America; spread to many countries within the last 30 years mainly via trade in foliage plants, and now occurs in Europe and South-East Asia. Increasing problem in greenhouse cultivation; often present on greenhouse weeds.
crops: Sweet pepper, Rose, Gerbera, Impatiens, Ornamentals
effects: Lives exclusively on leaves, staying mainly along veins on the lower parts of plants (prefers underside of leaves, though also found on upper surface). Completes its ENTIRE development from egg to adult on plant leaves (unlike F. occidentalis or T. tabaci which pupate in soil).
targets: Difficult to control because standard predatory mites and Orius are less effective against it and adults are poor fliers rarely caught on sticky traps; Anystis baccarum (whirligig mite) and Chrysoperla spp. can suppress foliar hotspots.
appearance: Adults found on both upper and undersides of leaves. Females are ~1.6 mm long; males are ~1.3 mm long. Dark brown to black with orange pigmentation between abdominal segments; dark wings are white at the base, which distinguishes this species from most other greenhouse thrips.
lifeCycle: Sexual or parthenogenetic reproduction; populations consist of more females than males (ratio varies). At 25°C, females lay an average of 77 eggs and live for an average of 41 days.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Deposited in the leaf tissue. At 25°C, females lay an average of 77 eggs. Subsequent stages are found on upper and undersides of leaves.
stageBreakdown.Larva, Pre-pupae, Pupae: White or light yellow; prefer the underside of leaves. Pupation occurs directly on the leaf (underside). Pre-pupae remain immobile and only move if disturbed.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females ~1.6 mm, males ~1.3 mm. Dark brown to black with orange pigmentation between segments and distinctive white wing bases.

conditions: Temperature thresholds: At 15°C, no oviposition occurs and most juveniles fail to complete development. Above 35°C, thrips stop laying eggs and juvenile survival is very low. Below 0°C, cannot survive for more than a few hours, making overwintering outside greenhouses impossible in temperate climates.

rows: Lethal within a few hours (cannot overwinter outdoors in temperate climates)

damage: Patchy silvering/discolouration in spots where cell contents are sucked out. In sweet pepper, damage appears as discolouration of older leaves at the bottom of the plant. High infestations cause leaves to shrivel entirely and fall off. Outside of ripe fruit takes on a silvery sheen.
usage: Monitoring Challenge: Does not move very much unless disturbed. Because adults are poor fliers and rarely caught on sticky traps, finding infestations requires careful manual leaf inspection (especially lower leaves and weeds), often going unnoticed until proportions are serious.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Li et al. (2012); Oetting & Beshear (1993); Opit et al. (1997)

synonyms: Liriomyza bryoniae, Liriomyza trifolii, Liriomyza huidobrensis, Liriomyza sativae
origin: Out of ~2,500 Agromyzidae species, only 11 are truly polyphagous. Species causing the most damage in crops under glass belong to the genus Liriomyza (containing over 300 very similar species).
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Lettuce, Melon, Cucumber, Celery, Pea, Bean, Potato, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Gypsophila, Ornamentals
effects: Adult females bore holes in the upper leaf surface with a toothed ovipositor to feed on plant sap (round feeding spots) and lay eggs (oval egg spots). Hatching larvae tunnel into mesophyll tissue creating serpentine or plate 'mines' while leaving outer epidermal layers intact.
targets: Controlled by parasitic wasps Diglyphus isaea (MIGLYPHUS - ectoparasitoid), Dacnusa sibirica (MINUSA - endoparasitoid), Opius pallipes, Diglyphus begini, predatory bug Macrolophus pygmaeus, and Steinernema feltiae.
appearance: Adults are small yellow and black coloured flies, at most several millimetres long. Colour varies slightly between Liriomyza species, requiring microscopic examination of male genitalia or molecular techniques for definitive identification.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, three larval instars (L1, L2, L3), pupal instar (with a brief pre-pupa stage), and adult fly. Populations typically consist of 50% females. Adults become active at sunrise, peak in the morning, and cease activity at dusk. Both males and females feed on flower nectar and honeydew (males lack an ovipositor and rely on females to create feeding punctures). Mating occurs within 1–2 days of emergence; a single mating fertilizes all laid eggs, though maximum fecundity requires multiple matings (unfertilized females lay no viable eggs).

stageBreakdown.Eggs & Feeding Spots: Females bore holes on upper leaf surface. Feeding spots are round (sap consumed, no egg laid); egg spots are oval and hard to detect.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (L1, L2, L3): Tunnel in mesophyll tissue without contacting outside air; older larvae make wider tunnels. If a leaf is too small, larvae can migrate through the leaf stalk to another leaf (cannot re-enter from outside).
stageBreakdown.Pre-pupa & Pupation: Unlike other leaf miners, Liriomyza larvae pupate in the ground rather than in leaf mines. Full-grown L3 larvae cut a sickle-shaped exit hole with mouthparts, crawl out in early morning (~1 hour later) as a pre-pupa, fall to the ground, and pupate at ~5 cm depth in soil or between plastic folds in artificial substrates (a small % pupates on leaf undersides). Pupae vary from light yellow to black.

conditions: Population development is influenced by temperature, light, host plant species/quality, parasitic wasps, population density, and humidity. Few adults develop in winter due to diapause or retarded development: L. bryoniae and L. huidobrensis pass through diapause and can overwinter outdoors in temperate climates, unlike L. trifolii.
damage: Direct Damage: Larval mining leads to desiccation, premature leaf-fall, cosmetic damage, and fruit sun-burning in (sub)tropical areas (e.g., tomato, melon). Seedlings and young plants can be totally destroyed. Adult feeding punctures reduce aesthetic value in ornamentals. Indirect Damage: Disease-causing fungi or bacteria enter plant tissue via feeding spots.

origin: Present in Europe, Asia, and Northern Africa. In Southern Europe it occurs outdoors, while in the rest of Europe it only occurs in greenhouses (common pest since the 1960s). Can remain present in greenhouses year-round.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Lettuce, Melon, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Larvae tunnel over the whole leaf, tunnels becoming wider as larvae grow, remaining mostly active in the upper mesophyll tissue.
targets: Controlled by Diglyphus isaea (MIGLYPHUS), Dacnusa sibirica (MINUSA), Opius pallipes, and Macrolophus pygmaeus.
appearance: Small, shiny yellow and black coloured flies with a yellow head, red eyes, and a conspicuous clear yellow dorsal thoracic shield. Ventral surface and legs are generally light yellow. Males measure ~1.5 mm; females measure 2–3 mm and feature a clearly visible black spot on the abdomen.
lifeCycle: Sex ratio is roughly 1:1. Mating takes place 1–2 days after adult emergence; pre-oviposition period lasts another 1–2 days. Males live for only a few days.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Milky-white and oval, measuring 0.1 x 0.3 mm long.
stageBreakdown.Larva 1: Transparent and freshly emerged from the egg, about 0.5 mm long.
stageBreakdown.Larva 2: Early second instar is a transparent, white colour, about 1.0 mm long, with the gut and its contents clearly visible.
stageBreakdown.Larva 3: Third instar remains a dirty white colour with a yellow head; gut contents are visible and green-black in colour. Full-grown larvae are 3–4 mm in length.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: Measures about 2 x 3 mm. Colour varies from golden yellow to dark brown, and even black. A proportion of pupae can survive over winter in temperate climates.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Shiny yellow and black flies; clear yellow dorsal thoracic shield; females 2–3 mm with black abdominal spot; males 1.5 mm.

conditions: Lower threshold for development is between 8°C and 10°C; above 35°C, development ceases.

damage: Pattern of damage depends on host plant. Larvae tunnel over the whole leaf in the upper mesophyll tissue, leading to desiccation and foliage loss.
usage: Develops faster than L. trifolii on tomato at both lower and warmer temperatures, making L. bryoniae the more frequent leaf miner pest in tomato.

origin: Originates in North America and is adapted to warmer climates. Found in Europe since ~1976 (introduced via infected chrysanthemum cuttings imported from Florida) and now distributed worldwide.
crops: Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Gypsophila, Celery, Sweet pepper, Pea, Bean, Potato, Tomato, Ornamentals
effects: Tunnels in leaf mesophyll. In gerbera, larvae eat outwards around the egg spot so mines join to form small 'plate mines'. Usually occurs in localized concentrations in the greenhouse.
targets: Controlled primarily by Diglyphus isaea (MIGLYPHUS). Note: Dacnusa sibirica has more difficulty controlling L. trifolii than L. bryoniae.
appearance: Very similar in appearance to L. bryoniae: adults and pupae are virtually indistinguishable, though adult L. trifolii have a slightly less shiny (more matte) appearance. Larvae are completely ochre-yellow in colour, particularly in the third instar (distinguishing them from dirty-white L. bryoniae larvae).
lifeCycle: Sex ratio varies from 2:1 to 1:1 (female:male). Males live only a few days. Lays far more eggs on chrysanthemum (275–300 eggs) than on tomato (max 80 eggs), and lives several days longer on chrysanthemum. Does not enter diapause and cannot overwinter outdoors in temperate climates.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: At first oval and transparent, later becoming cream-coloured; about 0.1–0.2 mm long.
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Unlike L. bryoniae, larvae are completely ochre-yellow in colour, especially in the last (3rd) instar.
stageBreakdown.Pupae & Adults: Virtually indistinguishable from L. bryoniae, though adults are slightly less shiny.

conditions: Lower development threshold lies between 8°C and 10°C; adapted to warmer regions. Develops more slowly than L. bryoniae on tomato at lower temperatures with higher mortality and lower reproductive capacity on tomato.

devTable.caption: Development Time (days) & Reproduction on Tomato at 60–70% RH (Minkenberg, 1990)

damage: Serpentine mines and plate mines (in gerbera), plus numerous adult female feeding punctures on ornamental foliage.
usage: Use Diglyphus isaea for biological control, as Dacnusa sibirica is less effective against L. trifolii.

origin: Originates from South and Middle America; spread over parts of the US and Hawaii since 1985, brought into northern Europe in 1989, and now occurs worldwide throughout the year.
crops: Lettuce, Pea, Chrysanthemum, Tomato, Leafy vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Females lay eggs on the upper leaf surface, where mining often begins, but larvae subsequently tunnel down toward the leaf underside along mid-veins and side-veins. Makes an enormous number of feeding spots (650/female in tomato to >1,300/female in chrysanthemum).
targets: Controlled by Diglyphus isaea (MIGLYPHUS) and Dacnusa sibirica (MINUSA).
appearance: Adults are slightly larger (2–3 mm) and darker in colour than L. bryoniae, but still feature the bright yellow dorsal thoracic shield. Larvae are slightly whiter than L. bryoniae (milky to yellowish-white) and lack the yellow head. Pupae (2–3 mm) vary from pale yellow to black in a single crop.
lifeCycle: At ~19°C, egg stage lasts 2 days, larval period 6 days, pupa 8 days, with a pre-oviposition period of 1–2 days (total life cycle 2 to 2.5 weeks at 19°C). Populations are well dispersed across the greenhouse even at low densities.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Laid in upper leaf tissue; hatch in ~2 days at 19°C (3.0 days at 27°C).
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Milky to yellowish-white and lack the yellow head of L. bryoniae.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: 2–3 mm long, varying from pale yellow to black. Can overwinter in a cold, empty greenhouse for at least 9 weeks (~90% mortality, but ~10% survive).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm long, darker than L. bryoniae with a bright yellow thoracic shield.

conditions: Slightly more cold-resistant than L. trifolii; pupae can overwinter in cold, empty greenhouses for 9+ weeks.

devTable.caption: Development on Chrysanthemum at 27°C and 50–60% RH (Parrella & Bethke, 1984)

damage: Mines run along mid-veins and side-veins or form large 'plate-mines' at the leaf base. Because most of the mine is on the leaf underside (especially at high temperatures), damage is less conspicuous and discovered later. Enormous numbers of feeding punctures (650 to >1,300 per female) cause greater crop damage than L. trifolii at high infestations.
usage: Inspect leaf undersides and leaf bases carefully; at lower temperatures mines are more often on the upper side.

origin: Widespread across North and South America, Australia, and other parts of the world, but not present in Europe.
crops: Tomato, Vegetables, Ornamentals, Cucurbits, Legumes
effects: Produces serpentine, tightly coiled mines of irregular shape that increase in width as larvae mature, plus adult feeding and egg-laying spots.
targets: Controlled by Diglyphus isaea (MIGLYPHUS) and naturally occurring Diglyphus begini in North America. Note: Dacnusa sibirica DOES NOT parasitize L. sativae.
appearance: Adults are very similar to Liriomyza huidobrensis. Larvae are yellow-orange in colour and resemble larvae of Liriomyza trifolii. Pupae vary from pale yellow-orange to golden brown and pupate in the soil.
lifeCycle: Eggs hatch in 2 to 5 days. Duration of larval development is 4 to 7 days at mean temperatures above 24°C. Larvae leave the leaves for pupation in the soil.
conditions: Adapted to warm conditions, but at temperatures above 30°C, the mortality rate of immature stages rises sharply.
damage: Tightly coiled, irregular serpentine mines and feeding punctures on foliage.
usage: Do not use Dacnusa sibirica against L. sativae; rely on Diglyphus isaea or Diglyphus begini.

origin: Appears very commonly in greenhouses throughout the world; Bradysia impatiens is present in Europe, Asia, and North and South America.
crops: Seedlings, Cuttings, Ornamentals, Soft fruits, Mushrooms, Vegetables, Greenhouse crops
effects: Larvae live in the ground and move very little, feeding mainly on decaying plant material, organic remains, algae, and fungi, as well as living root hairs, tender roots, and stem/leaf tissue. Adults are weak fliers that hardly feed during their ~1 week lifespan.
targets: Controlled by Steinernema feltiae (ENTONEM), Stratiolaelaps scimitus (ENTOMITE-M), Gaeolaelaps gillespiei (Gillespiei-Mite), Macrocheles robustulus (MACRO-MITE), and Dalotia coriaria (BioAtheta rove beetle). Facilitates invasion of pathogenic fungi (Fusarium, Botrytis, Verticillium).
appearance: Adults are 1–5 mm long grey-black midges with long 14-segmented antennae, long legs, and clear wing venation (males smaller than females). Larvae grow 5–12 mm long (0.5–1.5 mm diameter), legless, smooth 12-segmented cylindrical body (transparent at first, turning milky-white and opaque in L4) with a conspicuous shiny black head capsule equipped with biting-chewing mouthparts.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, four larval instars, pupa, and adult. Mating occurs within hours of emergence; females lay 50–300 eggs on damp soil close to roots with high organic/microbial activity. Pupation occurs in a small hole in the ground. Population is 50–70% females; adult lifespan is ~1 week.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Minute (0.1–0.25 mm), yellowish-white, laid on damp soil surface near plant roots (3–4 days at 25–29°C; do not hatch at 10°C or 35°C).

stageBreakdown.Pupae: 2–5 mm long, initially white turning yellow to brown; posterior end remains mobile. Takes 3–5 days at 25–29°C.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 1–5 mm grey-black midges with 14-segmented antennae and clear wing venation.

conditions: Active year-round in heated greenhouses (survives winter outdoors as larvae in temperate zones). Eggs do not hatch at 10°C or 35°C; at 32°C immature mortality is very high.

origin: Common worldwide in moist greenhouse environments where green algae grow.
crops: Cuttings, Seedlings, Ornamentals, Vegetables, Herbs, Greenhouse crops
effects: Larvae and adults feed on green algae and rotting organic plant material in moist substrates rather than feeding directly on living plant tissue.
targets: Controlled by Steinernema carpocapsae (Millenium / Capsanem), Steinernema feltiae (ENTONEM), Stratiolaelaps scimitus (ENTOMITE-M), Gaeolaelaps gillespiei, Macrocheles robustulus (MACRO-MITE), and Dalotia coriaria (BioAtheta rove beetle).
appearance: Small dark-bodied flies (robust build with short antennae and pale spots on dark wings), easily distinguished from slender long-legged fungus gnats.
lifeCycle: Consists of an egg, three larval instars, a pupa, and an adult fly. Eggs are laid singly and are bean-shaped. At 25°C, adult females live for approximately 25 days and can lay up to 500 eggs.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Bean-shaped and laid singly on moist algae-covered surfaces.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (3 Instars): Live in the ground and moist substrate surface, feeding on green algae, microorganisms, and rotting organic matter.
stageBreakdown.Pupae & Adults: Pupate in the substrate; adults live ~25 days and lay up to 500 eggs at 25°C.

conditions: Thrives in wet, over-irrigated areas with standing water and green algae growth. Egg-to-adult development takes ~43 days at 12°C and drops to 9–11 days at 25°C.

damage: Do not cause direct feeding damage to plants, but are a nuisance to greenhouse workers. Excreta (frass) deposited on leaves and petals causes cosmetic damage, high populations can retard the growth of young cuttings, and flies can transmit root-rot plant diseases.
usage: Cultural Control: Keeping greenhouse surfaces and substrates drier and preventing algal growth significantly reduces shore fly populations.

taxonomy: Order Diptera • Family Keroplatidae (Fungus Gnat Relatives)
origin: Major problem in potted orchids, especially in greenhouses in the Netherlands and international orchid production.
crops: Orchids, Phalaenopsis, Potted ornamentals
effects: Omnivorous larvae live between the roots and bark inside orchid pots, spinning highly acidic webs (pH <= 2.7) coated with oxalic-acid-containing saliva droplets to catch and kill soil mites, sciarid larvae, and springtails while also damaging orchid root tips.
targets: There are currently NO effective biological control natural enemies for controlling keroplatid flies.
appearance: Adult flies are elongate and slender, distinguished to species by wing patterns and markings. In Lyprauta cambria, eggs are greyish-black and spherical; larvae are worm-like, transparent greyish-white with brown or reddish heads; pupae are white to yellow inside a dense web.
lifeCycle: Consists of spherical eggs, omnivorous web-spinning larval stages living in bark substrate, pupae inside dense webs, and slender winged adults.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Greyish-black and spherical (in Lyprauta cambria).
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Transparent greyish-white with brown or reddish heads; live between orchid roots and bark, spinning acidic webs (pH 2.7 or less) with oxalic-acid saliva droplets for shelter and hunting prey.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: White to yellow, formed within a dense web inside the pot.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Elongate, slender fungus-gnat-like flies with distinct species-specific wing markings.

conditions: Humid, bark-based potted orchid substrates containing soil micro-arthropod prey and active root tips.
damage: Larvae cause superficial damage to orchid roots, particularly root tips, which turn black and begin to rot internally. Just above the damaged tip, roots produce large numbers of new lateral branches, resulting in fewer flower stems and a prolonged vegetative stage. Root lesions also create entry points for pathogens.
usage: Do not confuse with true potworms (small white earthworms of family Enchytraeidae). Inspect bark media for acidic webbing and blackened, branching root tips.

origin: Originally from Asia (China, Japan, and Korea); invaded North and South America and Europe starting in 2008/2009. Colonizes commercial fruit crops from neighbouring wild hosts, moving from early-ripening to later-ripening crops and lower to higher altitudes.
crops: Berries, Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherries, Plums, Stone fruits, Grapes
effects: Unlike other Drosophila species that only attack overripe/rotting fruit, D. suzukii females possess a strong, double-serrated, saw-like ovipositor capable of penetrating the skin of healthy, ripening, unharvested fruits. Larvae feed internally, causing rapid fruit collapse.
targets: There are currently NO effective commercial biological control natural enemies for controlling spotted wing drosophila.
appearance: Small flies (~2–3 mm long with a 6–8 mm wingspan). Males are smaller than females and easily distinguished by a prominent dark spot near the tip of each wing. Females lack wing spots but feature a heavily sclerotized, double-serrated saw-like ovipositor.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, three larval instars (L1, L2, L3), pupa, and adult fly. Sex ratio is 1:1. Adult females live 2–6 weeks at 22°C and lay <100 to nearly 400 viable eggs depending on host fruit and humidity.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: White, averaging 0.6 x 0.2 mm, with two respiratory filaments (breathing tubes) extending from one end that protrude out of the fruit skin (~1.5 days at 22°C).
stageBreakdown.Larvae (3 Instars): White to cream maggots developing inside the fruit; L1 (~0.7 mm, ~1 day at 22°C), L2 (~2.1 mm, ~1.5 days at 22°C), and L3 (~3.9 mm, ~3 days at 22°C).
stageBreakdown.Pupae: Tan-brown, ~3 mm long; pupate either fully/partly inside the fruit or outside on the ground (~6 days at 22°C).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm long (6–8 mm wingspan); males have a dark spot on each wing; females have a double-serrated ovipositor.

conditions: Optimal temperature for population growth is 21–22°C. Sensitive to high heat and low humidity: flies hide in cool, humid canopy refuges during the day and restrict flight/oviposition to morning and evening. Mortality is very high <= 10°C, immature development is impossible > 30°C, and adults die at 35°C. Overwinters as mated adult females in reproductive diapause.

synonyms: Black vine weevil (Otiorhynchus sulcatus), Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica), White grubs
origin: Major soil-dwelling root pests in temperate berry fields, nurseries, turfgrass, and container ornamentals across Canada and North America.
crops: Strawberry, Berries, Raspberry, Blueberry, Cranberry, Rhododendron, Azalea, Cyclamen, Taxus, Turfgrass, Nurseries, Ornamentals
effects: Nocturnal adult weevils chew characteristic marginal notches in leaves, while soil-dwelling C-shaped larvae (grubs) devour roots, crowns, and stem bases, girdling and killing plants.
targets: Larvae and grubs in the root zone are controlled by cruiser-type entomopathogenic nematodes Heterorhabditis bacteriophora (active 16–35°C), plus Steinernema feltiae, Steinernema carpocapsae, and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Black vine weevil adults (~8–10 mm) are dull black, flightless, all-female weevils with a short snout and fused wing covers. Larvae are legless, cream-white, curved C-shaped grubs with tan-brown head capsules.
lifeCycle: Adults emerge in late spring, feed nocturnally on leaf margins, and lay hundreds of eggs in soil near plant crowns. Larvae hatch and feed on root hairs and bark through summer and autumn, overwintering in soil before pupating in spring.
conditions: Soil temperatures of 15–30°C and moist, well-drained media favor both root-feeding grubs and entomopathogenic nematode application.
damage: Leaf-edge notching by adults; severe wilting, root pruning, crown girdling, and sudden plant collapse caused by larvae feeding underground.
usage: Drench root zone with Heterorhabditis bacteriophora when soil temperatures exceed 15–16°C (late summer/early autumn or spring), keeping media moist and avoiding UV exposure.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems; Biobest

origin: Originally from tropical and subtropical America (probably Brazil or Mexico); major pest in greenhouses worldwide since the late 19th century (first noted on greenhouse tomatoes in North America in 1870).
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Bean, Rose, Gerbera, Poinsettia, Ornamentals
effects: Larvae and adults extract large quantities of phloem sap and excrete excess sugar as sticky honeydew, encouraging black sooty moulds (Cladosporium spp.) and transmitting plant viruses such as Tomato Chlorosis Virus (ToCV).
targets: Optimal host for Encarsia formosa (EN-STRIP); also controlled by Eretmocerus eremicus (ERCAL), Macrolophus pygmaeus (MIRICAL), Nesidiocoris tenuis (NESIBUG), Dicyphus hesperus, Delphastus catalinae (DELPHIBUG), Amblyseius swirskii, Amblydromalus limonicus, Transeius montdorensis, Anystis baccarum, Nabis americoferus, Lecanicillium muscari (MYCOTAL), and Beauveria bassiana (BOVERIL).
appearance: Adults are ~1.1 mm long (males ~0.9 mm). Newly emerged adults are transparent-white without wax; within a few hours, the body and two pairs of wings are covered with white waxy powder. Wings are held horizontally forming a triangle from above. Mostly found in the top of the plant on undersides of topmost leaves.
lifeCycle: Six distinct developmental stages: egg, four larval instars (L1 crawler, L2, L3, L4/pupa), and adult. Females begin laying eggs 1–2 days after emergence (unmated females produce exclusively males; mated females produce ~50% females; parthenogenetic strains exist). Lifespan varies from several days to >2 months.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Elliptical, ~0.25 mm. Initially white (often dusted with wax powder), turning dark brown to black after 1–2 days. Deposited on undersides of young upper leaves, often in a circle on smooth leaves, fixed to the leaf with a short hook.
stageBreakdown.Larva 1 (Crawler): ~0.3 mm long with well-developed legs and antennae; mobile for several hours to find a feeding spot before becoming sessile. Virtually transparent.
stageBreakdown.Larva 2 & Larva 3: 0.3–0.4 mm long; legs and antennae reduced to 1–2 segments and no longer visible; remain flattened on leaf.
stageBreakdown.Larva 4 (Puparium / Pupa): Initially flat, later becoming a box-like, oval white case (~0.7 mm long) encircled by a wreath/ring of erect waxy rods and long dorsal wax filaments. Red eyes become visible inside. Adult emerges through a T-shaped dorsal fissure.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~1.1 mm (males 0.9 mm), white waxy powder, triangular outline from above; congregate at top of plant.

conditions: Optimal development temperature is 20–25°C. Better adapted to lower temperatures than Bemisia tabaci and suffers higher mortality at high temperatures. Has no special overwintering stage, but survives on cold-hardy plants (eggs survive >15 days at -3°C; older instars survive down to -6°C).

damage: Large populations retard growth, cause leaves to wilt/drop in full sunlight, and reduce yield. Honeydew makes fruit sticky, traps dirt, and promotes sooty moulds (Cladosporium spp.) that block photosynthesis and render fruit unmarketable. Transmits Tomato Chlorosis Virus (ToCV).
usage: Check undersides of topmost young leaves for circular egg rings and white waxy adults. Parasitized pupae turn black when parasitized by Encarsia formosa, or yellow when parasitized by Eretmocerus eremicus.

synonyms: Biotype B / MEAM1 (Poinsettia strain / Bemisia argentifolii), Biotype Q / MED (Mediterranean strain), Biotype A (Cotton strain)
taxonomy: Order Hemiptera • Family Aleyrodidae • Subfamily Aleyrodinae
origin: First described on tobacco in Greece in 1889; found in most tropical and subtropical countries worldwide (original habitat likely Pakistan/subtropics). Consists of a complex of at least 24 morphologically indistinguishable cryptic species/biotypes, with Biotypes B and Q being the most invasive and pesticide-resistant.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Poinsettia, Gerbera, Hibiscus, Bean, Squash, Ornamentals
effects: Phloem sap feeding, honeydew excretion, injection of phytotoxic enzymes that alter plant physiology (causing irregular fruit ripening and silverleaf), and transmission of >25 plant viruses including Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV).
targets: Controlled by Eretmocerus eremicus (ERCAL - superior to E. formosa on B. tabaci), Eretmocerus mundus, Macrolophus pygmaeus, Nesidiocoris tenuis, Dicyphus hesperus, Delphastus catalinae, Amblyseius swirskii, Amblydromalus limonicus, Transeius montdorensis, Anystis baccarum, Nabis americoferus, Lecanicillium muscari, and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Adults are slightly smaller than T. vaporariorum (< 1 mm), appear yellower due to less wax secretion, and hold wings vertically/roof-like along the body (appearing more elongated and narrow from above). Distributed over the WHOLE plant rather than just the top.
lifeCycle: Egg, four larval instars (L1 crawler, L2, L3, L4/pupa), and adult. Mating occurs 1–2 days after emergence (pre-oviposition 1–3 days); unmated females produce only males. Females lay 4–11 eggs/day and live 10–15 days up to several weeks.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Light yellow-green when newly laid, gradually turning light brown (average 0.18 mm). Spread widely over the underside of leaves across the whole plant (rarely in circles).
stageBreakdown.Larva 1, 2 & 3: L1 crawler (~0.25 mm) has legs and antennae and settles quickly; L2 and L3 are flat and scale-like, hardly distinguishable from T. vaporariorum.
stageBreakdown.Larva 4 (Pupa): Broad, flat, and transparent or yellow in colour (adult inside with red eyes and white wing buds is clearly visible). Lacks the wreath of erect waxy rods seen in T. vaporariorum, and has irregular, dented outlines conforming to leaf hairs.
stageBreakdown.Adults: < 1 mm, yellow body, wings held roof-like/vertical against body.

conditions: Optimum development temperature is 25–30°C. Above 30°C population growth declines; below 16°C it comes to a standstill, and at 9°C larvae die. Cannot survive below 0°C without a host plant.
damage: Honeydew and sooty mould (Cladosporium spp.). Injects enzymes causing severe physiological disorders even at very low whitefly densities: uneven ripening in tomatoes (green/yellow patches where fruit stays hard, sour, and pale inside—affected fruit will not recover even after whiteflies are controlled), yellowing of flower stalks in gerbera, silverleaf in squash, and irregular leaf yellowing in French beans. Vectors >25 viruses, most notably Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV). Highly resistant to chemical insecticides.
usage: When parasitized by Encarsia formosa, B. tabaci pupae turn brown (not black) with the parasite visible inside; when parasitized by Eretmocerus eremicus, pupae turn transparent yellow.

synonyms: Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, Macrosiphum euphorbiae, Aulacorthum solani
taxonomy: Order Hemiptera • Superfamily Aphidoidea • Family Aphididae
origin: Worldwide in outdoor and protected greenhouse crops.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Melon, Aubergine, Strawberry, Chrysanthemum, Rose, Begonia, Ornamentals, Vegetables
effects: Nymphs and adults extract phloem sap, disrupt plant growth hormone balance, excrete excess sugar as sticky honeydew, and transmit plant viruses (such as Potato Virus Y in tomato and Cucumber Mosaic Virus in cucumber, transmitted primarily by winged alate aphids).
targets: Controlled by parasitic wasps (Aphidius colemani, A. matricariae, A. ervi, Praon volucre, Ephedrus cerasicola, Aphelinus abdominalis), predators (Adalia bipunctata, Hippodamia convergens, Coleomegilla maculata, Didion longulum, Aphidoletes aphidimyza, Eupeodes americanus, Chrysoperla carnea, C. rufilabris, Micromus variegatus, Hemerobius spp., Macrolophus pygmaeus, Dicyphus hesperus, Nabis americoferus, Orius spp., Anystis baccarum), and entomopathogenic fungi (Beauveria bassiana).
appearance: Soft-bodied insects developing into either wingless adults (apterous) or winged adults (alate, with two pairs of wings where the forewings are significantly larger). Young nymphs moult four times before adulthood, leaving conspicuous white shed cuticles on foliage that reveal their presence.
lifeCycle: Greenhouse populations consist of viviparous females reproducing asexually (parthenogenetically), birthing genetically identical live nymphs where traits like colour morphs or pesticide resistance remain fixed. Because embryos begin developing inside a female before she is born ('telescoping generations'), females produce 3–10 nymphs/day over several weeks (40–100 total offspring). Outdoors, holocyclic species alternate between woody winter hosts (where sexual oviparae and males mate to lay overwintering eggs that hatch into a fundatrix) and herbaceous summer hosts; in greenhouses, most follow an anholocyclic (continuous asexual) cycle year-round, though overwintering eggs can occur in cold crops like strawberry.

stageBreakdown.Live Nymphs (4 Instars): Born as developed nymphs that feed immediately; moult 4 times and leave white shed skins (exuviae) on leaves.
stageBreakdown.Wingless Adults (Apterous): Develop under uncrowded conditions with high host quality for rapid localized colony build-up.
stageBreakdown.Winged Adults (Alate): Triggered primarily by crowding and declining plant quality; capable of travelling hundreds of kilometres on atmospheric thermals and high-altitude airstreams.

conditions: Under optimal conditions (~23°C), newly born aphids reach reproductive maturity in just 6–7 days.
damage: Retarded growth, deformed leaves, reduced yield, and death of young plants. Saliva induces strong toxic/allergic malformations in growing tips. Honeydew contaminates fruit/flowers and supports black sooty moulds (Cladosporium spp.) that block photosynthesis. Vectors PVY, CMV, and PLRV.
usage: Host Selection & Scouting: Aphids evaluate leaves visually (preferring yellowish-green young leaves; scent only operates at <1 m), perform a brief exploratory phloem probe, and move to the leaf underside. Scout early scattered colonists and white shed cuticles before crowding triggers winged dispersal.

metabolite: Green Peach Aphid / Peach Potato & Tobacco Aphid
synonyms: Peach potato aphid (M. persicae subsp. persicae), Tobacco aphid (M. persicae subsp. nicotianae)
origin: Probably originated in Asia (where its winter-hardy host, the peach tree, is native); now has a cosmopolitan worldwide distribution and occurs year-round in greenhouses.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Potato, Aubergine, Brassicas, Beet, Tobacco, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Highly polyphagous (>40 plant families). Distributed across the entire plant in closely packed colonies in flowers and on young leaves (M. p. nicotianae forms denser colonies closer to the top of the plant). Extracts sap, secretes honeydew, injects toxic saliva, and walks between plants. M. p. persicae is the most important viral vector among all aphids, transmitting >100 plant viruses (including PLRV and PVY).
targets: Vectors >100 viruses including Potato Leafroll Virus (PLRV) and Potato Virus Y (PVY). Controlled by Aphidius colemani, Aphidius matricariae, Aphelinus abdominalis, Ephedrus cerasicola, Adalia bipunctata, Hippodamia convergens, Coleomegilla maculata, Didion longulum, Eupeodes americanus, Micromus variegatus, Chrysoperla carnea, C. rufilabris, Macrolophus pygmaeus, Dicyphus hesperus, Nabis americoferus, Orius spp., Anystis baccarum, and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Oval-shaped, 1.2–2.1 mm long, with a matte (never glossy) appearance. M. p. persicae can be green, white-green, light yellow-green, grey-green, pink, or red; wingless M. p. nicotianae are always pink or red (colour alone cannot distinguish subspecies). Winged alates have a brown-black head/thorax and yellow-green to reddish abdomen with a dark brown dorsal patch and transverse black bands. Short legs, small finger-shaped cauda, long antennae reaching the cornicles, and clearly visible frontal tubercles pointing toward each other. Cornicles are medium-length, slightly swollen in the distal half, light-coloured with a dark tip.
lifeCycle: In temperate regions, M. p. persicae overwinters as eggs on peach/plum twigs (or as viviparous females in mild winters); no males are known in M. p. nicotianae. In greenhouses, both subspecies reproduce asexually year-round.

stageBreakdown.Nymphs: 4 nymphal instars, shedding white cuticles at each moult; mature rapidly at 20–25°C.
stageBreakdown.Wingless Adults (Apterous): 1.2–2.1 mm, matte green, yellow-green, pink, or red; converging frontal tubercles and slightly swollen light cornicles with dark tips.
stageBreakdown.Winged Adults (Alate): Brown-black head and thorax; green/reddish abdomen with dark dorsal patch and transverse black bars.

conditions: Optimal development occurs between 20°C and 25°C (population doubling time of just 2.7 days at 20°C on Chinese cabbage). At 30°C, mortality rises significantly and reproduction slows down.

damage: Stunted shoot growth, leaf curling, honeydew excretion, black sooty mould, toxic salivary reactions, and transmission of >100 persistent and non-persistent plant viruses.
usage: Scout growing points, flowers, and young leaf undersides early. Release Aphidius colemani or Aphidius matricariae at the very start of infestation.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Davis et al. (2006)

origin: Occurs worldwide with a preference for warmer regions and higher temperatures; comprises multiple strains varying in host association and insecticide resistance (host alternation reported only in North America).
crops: Cucumber, Melon, Cucurbits, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Chrysanthemum, Kalanchoe, Cotton, Citrus, Ornamentals
effects: Extremely polyphagous (>700 host plant species). Prefers young shoots, young leaves, and leaf undersides. Extracts phloem sap, secretes honeydew, injects toxic saliva, and transmits >50 plant viruses including Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV).
targets: Controlled by Aphidius colemani, Adalia bipunctata, Hippodamia convergens, Didion longulum, Eupeodes americanus, Micromus variegatus, Aphidoletes aphidimyza, Chrysoperla carnea, C. rufilabris, and entomopathogenic fungi. Note: Aphidius matricariae DOES NOT parasitize Aphis gossypii.
appearance: Distinguished from other aphids by having red eyes, relatively short antennae, and two cornicles (siphunculi) that are ALWAYS BLACK regardless of body colour. Body colour and size vary with temperature, food source, and density: large individuals (up to 1.8 mm) are dark green to black, whereas individuals in overcrowded colonies at high temperatures can be as small as 0.9 mm and yellow or cream-coloured.
lifeCycle: Females produce 3–10 young per day. Within 7 days, a population can multiply 4-fold on aubergine and up to 12-fold on cucumber.
conditions: Thrives in warm conditions; nymphal development on cucumber takes 9.6 days at 16°C and 6.5 days at 28°C. Can appear very early in the greenhouse season and build enormous populations within weeks, with peak damage at the start of summer.

rows: 4x on Aubergine; up to 12x on Cucumber

damage: Severe stunting, leaf distortion, heavy honeydew and sooty mould (Cladosporium spp.), and transmission of >50 viruses including Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV).
usage: Use Aphidius colemani for preventive parasitism (do not rely on A. matricariae) and predators like Adalia bipunctata for hotspots.

origin: Widespread greenhouse and field pest globally.
crops: Tomato, Potato, Aubergine, Sweet pepper, Solanaceous crops, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Colonizes Solanaceae and ornamental crops, extracting phloem sap, distorting growing tips, excreting honeydew, and transmitting plant viruses.
targets: Controlled by Aphelinus abdominalis, Praon volucre, Aphidius ervi, Adalia bipunctata, Didion longulum, Eupeodes americanus, Micromus variegatus, and Chrysoperla spp. (not parasitized by Aphidius colemani).
appearance: Large, elongated pear-shaped aphids (green or pink/reddish forms) with long legs, long antennae, and long cornicles.
lifeCycle: Viviparous parthenogenetic reproduction in greenhouses with 4 nymphal moults leaving conspicuous white shed cuticles.
conditions: Thrives in greenhouse vegetable and ornamental crops.
damage: Growth retardation, leaf curling, honeydew/sooty mould, and virus transmission.
usage: Target with Aphelinus abdominalis, Praon volucre, or Aphidius ervi rather than Aphidius colemani.

origin: Widespread pest in greenhouses and temperate crops.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Potato, Solanaceous crops, Begonia, Ornamentals
effects: Feeds on Solanaceae and ornamentals (such as begonia), injecting toxic saliva that causes severe leaf curling, yellow blotching, and growth malformation even at low densities.
targets: Controlled by Aphelinus abdominalis, Aphidius ervi, Praon volucre, Adalia bipunctata, Didion longulum, Eupeodes americanus, and Micromus variegatus (not parasitized by Aphidius colemani).
appearance: Medium-to-large globular aphid, shiny green to yellowish-green with darker green spots at the base of the cornicles.
lifeCycle: Asexual viviparous reproduction year-round in greenhouses.
conditions: Common in cool to moderate greenhouse temperatures.
damage: Severe salivary toxicity, leaf yellowing and malformation, honeydew, sooty mould, and virus transmission.
usage: Release Aphelinus abdominalis or Aphidius ervi early in the infestation.

origin: Likely originated in China; now distributed worldwide with extensive morphological variation and geographic races. Most common mealybug species encountered in horticulture.
crops: Fruit trees, Citrus, Ornamentals, Ficus, Palms, Schefflera, Croton, Kalanchoe, Rose, Gerbera, Cucumber, Melon, Aubergine
effects: Highly polyphagous phloem feeder found across all plant parts with a strong preference for growing tips and leaf axils. Extracts sap, excretes honeydew, and causes leaf yellowing and drop.
targets: Controlled by Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (Mealybug Destroyer), Anagyrus vladimiri, Leptomastix dactylopii, Lindorus lophanthae, Chrysoperla rufilabris, Adalia bipunctata, Dalotia coriaria (soil/root mealybugs), and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Adult females are oval, soft-bodied, 2.5–4 mm long and 2–3 mm wide, covered in fine white waxy powder through which the light yellow to pink body colour and a darker longitudinal dorsal stripe are visible. Easily distinguished by 18 pairs of relatively short wax rods of roughly equal length around the body margin and two short tail filaments always <20% of the body length. Adult males are tiny, winged, short-lived, and lack mouthparts (unable to feed).
lifeCycle: Sex ratio is 1:1. Fertilized females deposit 100–600 eggs over 1–2 weeks into an elongated cottony egg sac (ovisac). Female nymphs pass through 3 mobile instars; male nymphs pass through 2 feeding instars before forming a pre-pupa and pupa inside a white cottony cocoon.

stageBreakdown.Eggs & Ovisac: 100–600 eggs laid over 1–2 weeks inside an elongated white cottony egg sac; egg development is strongly influenced by humidity.
stageBreakdown.1st Instar (Crawlers): 0.5–0.7 mm long, highly mobile; actively disperse across the plant and along crop wires to find feeding sites.
stageBreakdown.2nd & 3rd Instar Nymphs: L2 nymphs become darker and less active. Male L2 nymphs spin a white cottony cocoon to pupate; female nymphs remain mobile through L3 to adulthood.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Females 2.5–4 mm, wingless, oval with 18 pairs of equal marginal wax filaments; males tiny, winged, non-feeding.

conditions: Egg-to-adult development in greenhouses takes ~1–2 months (30–60 days) depending on temperature, host plant quality, and relative humidity. All biological development ceases below ~8°C, and egg-laying ceases below 13°C. Overwinters in the ground in the nymphal stage without entering true diapause.
