rows: 100–600 eggs / female over 1–2 weeks (1:1 sex ratio)

damage: Stunted growth, wilting, premature leaf yellowing and drop, cottony wax accumulation in leaf axils and fruit stalks, and honeydew/sooty mould contamination.
usage: Scout hidden leaf axils, growing tips, pot rims, and crop wires where mobile L1 crawlers disperse. Pair parasitoids (Anagyrus vladimiri, Leptomastix dactylopii) for ongoing suppression with Cryptolaemus montrouzieri for dense hotspots.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Invasive East Asian polyphagous pest established in British Columbia and North America; attacks tree fruits, berries, fruiting vegetables, and ornamentals, and aggregates inside structures in autumn.
crops: Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Berries, Vineyards, Grapes, Sweet pepper, Tomato, Sweet Corn, Bean, Legumes, Ornamentals
effects: Pierces fruit, pods, buds, and stems with a long, slender plant-feeding beak (rostrum), injecting digestive enzymes that cause corky sunken spots ('cat-facing'), seed abortion, and unmarketable fruit.
targets: Distinguish carefully from the beneficial Spined Soldier Bug (Podisus maculiventris): H. halys is larger (12–17 mm), has rounded/blunt shoulders, characteristic white bands on the antennae, obvious alternating light/dark bands along the abdomen edge, and a long slender beak. Natural enemies include egg parasitoids (Trissolcus japonicus), Tachinid flies, and generalist predators.
appearance: Adult 12–17 mm mottled brown shield-shaped bug with rounded/smooth shoulders (humeral angles), distinct alternating light/white bands on the antennae, strong black-and-white checkering along the exposed abdominal margin (connexivum), and a long slender piercing beak. Eggs are barrel-shaped and pale green/white laid in tight clusters on leaf undersides; nymphs have bright orange/red and black markings and banded legs/antennae.
lifeCycle: Overwinters as adults in sheltered structures and wooded edges -> spring females lay clusters of ~28 eggs -> 5 nymphal instars -> adult (~36 days egg-to-adult at 25°C; 1–2 generations/year in temperate Pacific Northwest climates).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Clusters of ~20–30 pale green/white barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs: 5 instars progressing from orange-red/black tick-like 1st instars to mottled brown/black nymphs with white antennal and tibial bands.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 12–17 mm marbled brown shield bug with rounded shoulders and white-banded antennae (distinguish from beneficial Podisus maculiventris).

conditions: Active 15–35°C (optimum development ~25–30°C; developmental threshold ~14°C).
damage: Sunken corky lesions ('cat-facing') on apples, stone fruit, and peppers; cloudy spot blemishes on tomatoes; pod deformity and seed loss; foul defensive odour and nuisance indoor overwintering aggregations.
usage: Monitor perimeter traps and borders, confirm species ID (smooth shoulders + white antennal bands = pest BMSB; pointed shoulders + unbanded antennae + thick beak = beneficial Podisus maculiventris), and conserve Tachinid and egg parasitoids.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM; Koppert Biological Systems

synonyms: Paratrioza cockerelli, Potato psyllid, Tomato psyllid
origin: Native to western North America; significant pest in greenhouse tomatoes, peppers, aubergine, and field potatoes.
crops: Tomato, Potato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Solanaceous crops
effects: Phloem-feeding psyllid whose nymphs excrete white granular wax ('psyllid sugar'), inject saliva causing 'psyllid yellows' (upward leaf curling, chlorosis, stunting), and transmit Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (Zebra Chip disease in potato).
targets: Controlled by the specialist ectoparasitoid wasp Tamarixia triozae (which parasitizes older nymphs and host-feeds on young nymphs), Dicyphus hesperus, Orius insidiosus, Chrysoperla spp., Hemerobius spp., and Adalia bipunctata.
appearance: Adults (~2 mm) resemble tiny winged cicadas or aphids, black with a white dorsal band on the first and last abdominal segments and roof-like clear wings; nymphs are flat, scale-like, oval, green-to-orange with a fringe of short filaments around the margin.
lifeCycle: Tiny yellow stalked eggs laid mainly along leaf margins and undersides -> 5 flattened nymphal instars -> winged jumping adults (~15–21 days egg-to-adult at 20–26°C).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Minute yellow-orange football-shaped eggs suspended on short stalks along leaf edges.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (L1–L5): Flat, oval, scale-like yellow-green nymphs that anchor on leaf undersides and excrete white waxy granules.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Small (~2 mm) jumping black psyllids with clear roof-like wings and white abdominal bands.

conditions: Optimal development at 21–27°C (~15 days at 26°C); slows below 15°C and above 32°C.
damage: Psyllid yellows (purple-veined or yellow upward-curled leaves, rosetted shoots, small misshapen fruit), white 'psyllid sugar' honeydew pellets, sooty mould, and Zebra Chip bacterial transmission.
usage: Scout lower and mid-canopy leaf undersides for stalked eggs, flattened nymphs, and white sugar-like granules; release Tamarixia triozae early alongside Dicyphus hesperus.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems; UC IPM

metabolite: Armoured & Soft Scale Insects (California Red, Oleander & Brown Soft Scale)
scientificName: Aonidiella aurantii / Aspidiotus nerii / Coccus hesperidum
synonyms: California red scale (Aonidiella aurantii), Oleander scale (Aspidiotus nerii), San Jose scale (Comstockaspis perniciosa), Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum)
taxonomy: Order Hemiptera • Superfamily Coccoidea (Families Diaspididae & Coccidae)
origin: Cosmopolitan sap-sucking pests of citrus, tree fruits, woody ornamentals, palms, ferns, and tropical greenhouse crops.
crops: Citrus, Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Vineyards, Ornamentals, Palms, Ficus, Ferns, Schefflera, Rose
effects: Mobile 1st-instar crawlers disperse over leaves, stems, and fruit before settling into immobile wax-shielded nymphs and adults. Armoured scales (Diaspididae) secrete a detachable waxy cover and inject toxic saliva without producing honeydew; soft scales (Coccidae) retain an attached carapace and excrete abundant honeydew supporting black sooty mould.
targets: Controlled by the Scale Destroyer beetle Lindorus lophanthae (= Rhyzobius lophanthae), the armoured-scale ectoparasitoid wasp Aphytis melinus, Metaphycus helvolus (on soft brown scale), Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (on soft scales), Adalia bipunctata, and Chrysoperla larvae.
appearance: Armoured scales form flat circular or oyster-shell waxy shields (1.5–2.5 mm) loosely covering a flattened yellow-orange body underneath; soft scales (e.g., Coccus hesperidum) are 2–4 mm oval convex yellow-brown-to-mottled domes firmly attached to the insect body.
lifeCycle: Egg (or live-born crawler in some soft scales) -> mobile 6-legged 1st-instar 'crawler' that settles to feed -> sessile scale-covered nymphal instars -> mature sessile female (or tiny winged non-feeding male); typically ~30–65 days depending on species and temperature.

stageBreakdown.Crawlers (L1): Tiny oval yellow 1st instars with functional legs that disperse to new leaves and woody stems.
stageBreakdown.Sessile Nymphs: Secrete waxy scale armour (Diaspididae) or leathery carapace (Coccidae) and moult beneath it.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Wingless legless females beneath shield/shell; short-lived winged males.

conditions: Active year-round in heated greenhouses and tropical interiorscapes; development takes ~31–65 days across 18–30°C.
damage: Chlorotic halos, twig and branch dieback, heavy honeydew/sooty mould (soft scales), fruit cosmetic downgrading, and plant decline in palms and ornamentals.
usage: Time Lindorus lophanthae and Aphytis melinus releases with crawler and 2nd–3rd instar scale stages; avoid ant interference that protects honeydew-producing soft scales.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); UC IPM; Koppert Biological Systems

metabolite: Caterpillars & Moth Pests (Looper, Diamondback, Corn Borer, Codling Moth & Armyworms)
scientificName: Trichoplusia ni / Plutella xylostella / Ostrinia nubilalis / Cydia pomonella / Pieris rapae
synonyms: Cabbage looper (Trichoplusia ni), Diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella), European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), Codling moth (Cydia pomonella), Imported cabbageworm (Pieris rapae), Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda), Beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua), Tomato leafminer moth (Tuta absoluta), Leek moth (Acrolepiopsis assectella)
taxonomy: Order Lepidoptera (Families Noctuidae, Plutellidae, Crambidae, Tortricidae, Pieridae, Gelechiidae)
origin: Major defoliating, fruit-boring, and leaf-mining Lepidoptera pests spanning greenhouse vegetables, brassicas, corn, alliums, orchards, and berries.
crops: Brassica, Cabbage, Broccoli, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Sweet Corn, Corn, Onions, Leek, Apple, Orchards, Berries, Cranberry, Hop, Hemp, Ornamentals
effects: Larval caterpillars chew foliage, bore into stalks/ears/fruit, or mine leaves (Tuta absoluta), causing rapid defoliation, frass contamination, and direct fruit loss.
targets: Eggs parasitized by Trichogramma spp. (T. brassicae, T. minutum, T. ostriniae, T. pretiosum, T. platneri) and preyed on by Macrolophus pygmaeus, Nesidiocoris tenuis, Dicyphus hesperus, Orius spp., Chrysoperla spp., and Coleomegilla maculata. Young caterpillars parasitized by Cotesia spp. (C. marginiventris, C. vestalis, C. flavipes, C. glomerata) and Tachinid flies, preyed on by Podisus maculiventris, and infected by Steinernema carpocapsae, Bacillus thuringiensis, and Beauveria bassiana.
appearance: Moths/butterflies lay round or domed striated eggs (singly or in masses) on foliage; larvae are cylindrical caterpillars with 3 pairs of true thoracic legs and abdominal prolegs (loopers move in an arching 'inchworm' gait), spinning silken cocoons or pupating in debris/soil.
lifeCycle: Egg (3–7 d) -> 4–6 chewing caterpillar instars (10–25 d) -> pupa/chrysalis -> winged moth or butterfly (~18–42 days depending on species and temperature).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Targeted by Trichogramma spp. egg parasitoids before hatching (parasitized eggs turn charcoal-black).
stageBreakdown.Young Larvae (L1–L2): Targeted by Cotesia spp. koinobiont parasitoids, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), and predatory bugs.
stageBreakdown.Larger Caterpillars & Pupae: Attacked by Podisus maculiventris, Tachinid flies, and soil/foliar Steinernema carpocapsae.

conditions: Most greenhouse and summer field species develop rapidly between 15°C and 30°C (~18 days at 25°C).
damage: Windowpane feeding, ragged foliar holes, hollowed brassica heads, tunneled stalks/ears (European corn borer), wormy fruit (codling moth, Tuta absoluta), and dark fecal frass.
usage: Use pheromone traps and crop scouting to time Trichogramma egg-card hangs right at moth flight/oviposition, and pair with Cotesia spp., Podisus maculiventris, or Steinernema carpocapsae.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM
hostPlantsBeeSheet: Beta cicla; Brassica juncea; Brassica oleracea; Brassica oleracea (on leaves); Chaenomeles japonica; Glycine max; Lactuca sativa; Mentha; Petroselinum crispum; Smilax rotundifolia; Solanum; Spathiphyllum

origin: Accidentally imported into Germany from Chile in 1958; distributed worldwide for research and used commercially in greenhouses since 1967.
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Strawberry, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Specialized predator that feeds exclusively on spider mites (Tetranychus spp.). Feeds on all stages of spider mites with a strong preference for eggs. An adult female consumes up to 5 adult spider mites or 20 young larvae/eggs per day.
targets: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) and red spider mite (T. cinnabarinus).
appearance: Adult mites are bright orange-red, pear-shaped, with eight long legs and are highly active (especially at higher temperatures). Females are ~0.6 mm long; males are slightly smaller, flatter, and more elongated. Have NO eyes: rely entirely on sensory hairs/organs on their front legs (stirring up and down in the air) to register plant volatiles emitted by spider-mite-damaged plants and tactile sense to find prey.
lifeCycle: Five stages: egg (oval, colourless-pink, ~3 d), 6-legged non-feeding larva (~1.1 d), 8-legged protonymph & deutonymph (~3 d total), and adult (lifespan ~50 days; no overwintering diapause). Because its development rate is roughly twice as fast as T. urticae, predator populations increase rapidly to suppress pest outbreaks. At 25°C, adult females start laying eggs ~1 day after emergence, laying up to 5 eggs/day (population can double every 2 days).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, colourless to light pink (~3 d), approximately twice the size of spider mite eggs.
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Six-legged (~1.1 d); do NOT feed and remain inactive until molting into protonymphs.
stageBreakdown.Protonymph & Deutonymph: Eight-legged active feeding stages (~3 d combined).
stageBreakdown.Adults: Orange-red, ~0.6 mm long, 8 long legs, eyeless, very fast-moving (lifespan ~50 days; no overwintering).

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C; juvenile mortality rises sharply below 15°C and above 30–35°C). Humidity sensitivity: >=70% RH preferred (sensitive to dry conditions; RH <70% impairs egg hatching and drives P. persimilis down into lower humid foliage away from upper-canopy spider mites).
usage: Locates prey via scent (leaf damage volatiles and webbing). If prey is scarce, populations decline dramatically, and in complete absence of prey, P. persimilis becomes cannibalistic.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Occurs naturally in temperate and subtropical areas of North and South America and around the Mediterranean Sea. On the commercial market since 1985.
crops: Berries, Strawberry, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Fruit trees, Greenhouse vegetables, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Selective predator of tetranychid mites with a strong preference for spider mites (T. urticae), but also feeds and survives on tarsonemid mites (broad mite, cyclamen mite), thrips, or pollen. Can survive much longer than P. persimilis in the complete absence of food.
targets: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus), and Cyclamen/Strawberry mite (Phytonemus pallidus).
appearance: Resembles N. cucumeris, A. swirskii, and A. limonicus, with a flatter, more elongated body than P. persimilis (~0.4 mm). Lighter and transparent white color when young; ingested food shines through the skin, often showing an X-shaped marking on the back. If food is absent, they become thinner and uniformly light transparent.
lifeCycle: Stages: egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Mating is essential for oviposition. Oviposition period is ~20 days; females live another 2 weeks, laying 40–60 eggs total (2–3 eggs/day) with a female proportion of ~60%. Commercially available strains do not enter diapause (though wild strains in severe winter areas may).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Roughly 0.4 mm long, oval, transparent white, deposited on the underside of leaves.
stageBreakdown.Larvae & Nymphs: Feed mainly on spider mite eggs, larvae, and nymphs rather than adult mites.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Flat, elongated, pale cream to light orange/brown with a visible dorsal X-mark when fed; adult females feed on all stages of spider mites.

conditions: Active 13–32°C (~25°C best; egg-to-adult takes 3–4 days at 30–32°C, lower limit ~10°C, no eggs laid at 40°C). Tolerates 40–80% RH (best ~65–75% RH; more tolerant of dry conditions than many predatory mites, though RH < 70% still increases egg mortality).
usage: Uses volatiles emitted by spider-mite-damaged plants to locate prey. Stays in the crop longer at low prey densities due to starvation tolerance and broader diet, and is more tolerant to many synthetic pesticides than P. persimilis.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

taxonomy: Order Diptera • Family Cecidomyiidae (Predatory Gall Midge)
origin: Found almost worldwide; occurs spontaneously in numerous greenhouse and outdoor crops.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Specialized spider mite predator: ONLY the larvae feed on spider mites (Tetranychus urticae, T. turkestani, T. kanzawai, etc.). Immediately after hatching, larvae immobilize prey with mouthparts and suck out contents, consuming 15 adult spider mites or up to 50 mite eggs per day.
targets: Spider mite hotspots (Tetranychus urticae, T. cinnabarinus, T. turkestani, T. kanzawai).
appearance: Adults are small, rosy-brown midges with a light covering of hairs on wings and body. Male antennal segments are longer and hairier than the female's. Larvae are ~2 mm when full grown and orange/yellow/red depending on prey eaten.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg (3–5 d), 3 predatory larval instars (5–7 d), white silken cocoon/pupa on the leaf, and adult (~2–4 weeks total depending on temperature). ONLY the larvae (~2 mm orange/yellow-red) are predatory; adults live up to 14 days, require water/sugar (honeydew or nectar), and lay up to ~60 eggs on mite-infested leaves within 2 days of emergence (~60% female). Can overwinter in the pre-pupal stage in temperate regions.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Transparent to light yellow, slightly longer than spider mite egg diameter (3–5 d), banana-shaped, laid near leaf veins in spider mite colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (3 Instars): Newly emerged larva is yellowish-white, turning orange/red (~2 mm, 5–7 d). Only predatory life stage; can survive several days without food (inducing earlier pupation).
stageBreakdown.Pupae: Larvae spin a white cocoon near a leaf vein and pupate within it.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Small rosy-brown gall midges; strong fliers that locate spider mite colonies via plant volatiles.

conditions: Active 15–27°C (best 20–27°C; >30°C is harmful/lethal; development ceases below 8°C and eggs fail to hatch at 35°C). Requires >80% RH best for optimal control (development and juvenile survival decline below ~50–65% RH).
usage: Adults easily disperse by flight to find spider mite colonies via scent. Excellent for controlling spider mite hotspots, especially when combined with P. persimilis, N. californicus, or Stethorus punctillum.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

tradeNames: SWIRSKI-MITE, SWIRSKI-MITE PLUS, SWIRSKI-MITE LD, ULTI-MITE SWIRSKI
origin: Naturally occurring in the Mediterranean basin, Middle East, and Africa; introduced globally as a commercial biocontrol agent starting in 2005.
crops: Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Aubergine, Gerbera, Rose, Phalaenopsis, Palms, Schefflera, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predatory mite that pierces prey and sucks out contents. Preys on first instar thrips larvae (~4 F. occidentalis L1/day at 25°C), whitefly eggs (especially young white eggs <24h old), crawlers, and L2 larvae, plus spider mites, broad mites, cyclamen mites, flat mites (Brevipalpus spp.), and pollen.
targets: Thrips (first instar larvae), Whiteflies (eggs, crawlers, young larvae), Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus), Cyclamen mite (Phytonemus pallidus), False spider mites (Brevipalpus spp.), and Spider mites.
appearance: Adult mites have 8 legs and a flat, elongated body roughly 0.4 mm in length (males smaller than females). Colour varies from almost lucent whitish to opaque white or yellow depending on prey eaten. Very mobile on leaf undersides and often congregate in the axils of leaf veins to rest. Difficult to spot in the crop due to tiny size and colour.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Mating is essential for reproduction; sex ratio is 60–70% females. At 25°C, females lay 3–4 eggs/day on mixed diets (2.3 eggs/day on T. vaporariorum eggs; 1.4 eggs/day on F. occidentalis L1 larvae). Does NOT enter diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, white, ~0.14 mm in diameter; laid on the underside of leaves, often in the axil of veins. Sensitive to low humidity (only 50% hatch at 63% RH at 25°C).
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Have 6 legs, match the colour of eggs, and are only slightly larger. Like N. cucumeris, the larvae of A. swirskii DO NOT need to feed to develop into protonymphs.
stageBreakdown.Protonymph & Deutonymph: Larger than larvae, have 8 legs, and are a whitish-yellow colour.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.4 mm long, flat, elongated, translucent white to yellow; rest in vein axils.

conditions: Active ~18–32°C (best 20–32°C; poor performance below 18°C, and eggs fail to hatch at 13°C). Prefers >=60% RH (egg hatch declines considerably at low RH, though the leaf boundary layer on healthy well-watered plants mitigates ambient dryness). Cannot survive harsh winters outdoors in temperate areas.

usage: Can survive on pollen and leaf fluids in the absence of pests, allowing early preventive establishment in flowering crops like sweet pepper before thrips or whiteflies appear (not used on tomato). Performs best on mixed diets.

origin: First described from France; now distributed worldwide and widely used for biological control of thrips and tarsonemid mites in greenhouse crops.
crops: Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Aubergine, Strawberry, Cyclamen, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predatory mite; nymphs and adults pierce prey and suck out contents, feeding almost exclusively on first instar (L1) thrips larvae (~6 F. occidentalis L1 larvae/day per adult female at 25°C), plus broad mites, cyclamen mites, spider mites, and pollen.
targets: First instar thrips larvae (Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci), Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus), and Cyclamen/Strawberry mite (Phytonemus pallidus).
appearance: Adult females are light beige with a flat, elongated body roughly 0.4 mm long (males are smaller). Protonymphs, deutonymphs, and adults have 8 legs and are very mobile on leaf undersides. Difficult to spot in the crop due to size and beige colour.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Mating is essential. At 25°C, the oviposition period lasts 20–35 days, producing 30–50 eggs per female (~2 eggs/day on F. occidentalis L1). Sex ratio is 60–70% females. Commercial biocontrol strains do NOT enter diapause (allowing winter use in heated greenhouses under short day-length), though wild temperate strains do.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, white, ~0.14 mm in diameter; laid on leaf underside on leaf hairs (trichomes) or in vein axils.
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Have 6 legs, same colour as eggs, slightly larger. Do NOT need to feed to develop into protonymphs.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs & Adults: Nymphs have 8 legs and pale brown colour; adults are ~0.4 mm and light beige. Nymphs have more trouble capturing thrips than adults and sometimes partly consume thrips larvae killed by adults.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C; ineffective above 30°C). Humidity sensitivity: >=70% RH preferred for activity and egg survival (at 25°C and 65% RH only 50% of eggs survive, and below 60% RH eggs desiccate unless protected by the leaf boundary layer on well-watered plants).

usage: Can establish in pollen-bearing crops like sweet pepper before pests arrive.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Widespread in humid temperate to subtropical areas of North, Central, and South America, New Zealand, and Australia. Brought onto the market in 2012 after Koppert developed an economic mass-rearing system.
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Rose, Gerbera, Ornamentals
effects: Aggressive generalist predatory mite feeding on BOTH first and second instar thrips larvae (overwhelms more L2 F. occidentalis larvae than N. cucumeris or A. swirskii; eats ~7 L1 thrips/day at 25°C), plus whitefly eggs (especially young white eggs <24h old), crawlers, and nymphs, spider mites, tarsonemids, pollen, and plant sap.
targets: First and second instar thrips larvae (F. occidentalis, T. tabaci) and Whitefly eggs, crawlers, and young larvae (T. vaporariorum, B. tabaci).
appearance: Adult mites have 8 legs, a flat, elongated body roughly 0.4 mm in length (males smaller than females). Translucent white in colour, varying by prey or appearing greenish when taking fluids from leaves. Very mobile on leaf undersides.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Mating is essential; sex ratio is 60–70% females. At 25°C, females lay 3–4 eggs/day (3.7 eggs/day on young whitefly eggs, 1.2/day on older brown whitefly eggs, 3.3–3.4/day on whitefly crawlers/nymphs, ~3/day on thrips larvae). Does NOT enter diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, white, ~0.14 mm in diameter, laid on the underside of leaves. Sensitive to low humidity (only 50% hatch at 70% RH at 25°C).
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Have 6 legs, same colour as eggs, slightly larger. UNLIKE N. cucumeris and A. swirskii, the larvae of A. limonicus MUST FEED; without food they develop very slowly with high mortality.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs & Adults: Nymphs have 8 legs and are whitish-yellow/translucent white. Adults ~0.4 mm, translucent white or greenish.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C; remains active at cooler temperatures than A. swirskii with slow development possible from 10°C, and no development at 35°C). Prefers >=70% RH (sensitive to low RH, mitigated by the leaf boundary layer on well-watered plants).

usage: Superior to N. cucumeris and A. swirskii at cool temperatures (10–15°C) and against second-instar thrips larvae. Establish early with pollen (all crops except tomato).

origin: Naturally occurring in Australia and certain South Pacific islands; current commercial biological control agent in Canada, Europe, and worldwide.
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Gerbera, Rose, Strawberry, Ornamentals
effects: Aggressive generalist predatory mite feeding on BOTH 1st & 2nd instar thrips larvae (overwhelms more L2 F. occidentalis larvae than N. cucumeris or A. swirskii; adult female consumes ~10 L1 thrips larvae/day at 25°C), plus whitefly eggs and larvae, non-webbing spider mites, tarsonemid mites, and pollen.
targets: First and second instar thrips larvae (F. occidentalis, T. tabaci) and Whitefly eggs, crawlers, and young larvae.
appearance: Adult mites have 8 legs, a flat, elongated body roughly 0.4 mm in length (males smaller than females). Translucent white colour, varying to opaque white or yellow depending on prey eaten. Very mobile on leaf undersides.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and adult. Mating is essential; sex ratio is 60–70% females. At 25°C, females lay ~2.4 eggs/day on F. occidentalis L1 larvae and ~2 eggs/day on T. vaporariorum eggs. Does NOT enter diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, white, ~0.14 mm in diameter, laid on leaf undersides. Sensitive to low humidity (only 50% hatch at 70% RH at 25°C).
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Have 6 legs, same colour as eggs, slightly larger. UNLIKE N. cucumeris and A. swirskii, the larvae of T. montdorensis MUST FEED; without food they develop very slowly and mortality is high.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs & Adults: Nymphs have 8 legs and are whitish-yellow; adults are ~0.4 mm and translucent white to yellow.

conditions: Best at 20–32°C (ineffective <15°C; mites do not develop into adults at 10°C, nor do they develop at 35°C). Requires >=70% RH (sensitive below 70% RH in the leaf microclimate boundary layer for optimal egg hatch).

usage: High daily predation rate (~10 L1 thrips/day at 25°C) and establishes well on pollen in sweet pepper and ornamentals (all crops except tomato).

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Anthocoridae (Predatory Flower Bug)
origin: Widely distributed in Europe, Northern Africa, and the Middle East; successfully used for over 20 years, though more common commercially in European/Mediterranean programs than in Canadian greenhouse programs (where O. insidiosus predominates).
crops: Sweet pepper, Strawberry, Aubergine, Cucumber, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predatory bug that pierces prey with mouthparts and consumes body contents. Feeds on ALL plant-dwelling stages of thrips (larvae and adults), plus whiteflies, aphids, small caterpillars, spider mites, and pollen. Nymphs kill ~54 L2 F. occidentalis nymphs during development (~4/day); adult females kill up to 20 thrips nymphs or 6–7 adult thrips per day.
targets: All mobile stages of Thrips (Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci, Echinothrips americanus), plus aphids, spider mites, whiteflies, and moth eggs.
appearance: Adults are 1.4–2.4 mm long, brown to black with light grey-white spots on the wings, and conspicuous red compound eyes recognizable in all instars. Female abdomen is slightly larger and more robust than the male's.
lifeCycle: Consists of 7 developmental stages: egg, five nymphal instars (N1–N5), and adult. Mating occurs soon after emergence; oviposition starts 3–4 days later, peaking after a week at ~6 eggs/day. At 25°C, adults live 3–4 weeks and females lay >160 eggs when feeding on F. occidentalis. Sex ratio is 50–60% females. Northern wild strains undergo reproductive diapause, whereas southern and commercial strains DO NOT diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: About 0.4 mm long and 0.13 mm wide, colourless when laid, turning milky white. Embedded separately into plant tissue (leaf stem or main vein on leaf underside) with only a white, round operculum (lid) sticking out.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Newly emerged nymphs are shiny and almost colourless, turning yellow within hours. Later stages are yellowish-orange with orange-brown spots and conspicuous red eyes; young nymphs have an orange patch on the abdomen. Wing buds begin developing in N2 and are clearly visible in N5.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Immediately after final molt they are yellow (wings take ~1 hour to unfold), turning brown-black with grey-white spots after a few hours (1.4–2.4 mm long).

conditions: Active >20°C (best ~20–30°C; effectiveness reduced >30°C); >75% RH optimal under hot greenhouse conditions. Pollen enhances establishment when prey is scarce, though juvenile mortality is higher on pollen alone. Can be cannibalistic when prey is scarce.

usage: In pollen-producing plants, younger nymphs are mainly on leaves while older nymphs and adults are in flowers. Good fliers that actively search leaves damaged by thrips and react rapidly to disturbance.

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Anthocoridae (Insidious Flower Bug)
origin: Occurs naturally in Northern, Central, and South America; main North American and Canadian commercial Orius species for biological thrips control.
crops: Sweet pepper, Berries, Strawberry, Cucumber, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predatory bug feeding on ALL plant-dwelling stages of thrips (adult thrips as well as larvae), plus psyllids, whiteflies, aphids, small caterpillars, mites, and pollen. Adult females can eat ~20 Frankliniella occidentalis per day. Handling note: can occasionally bite people during scouting or leaf handling.
targets: All mobile stages of Thrips (larvae and adults of Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci) and Tomato/Potato psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli).
appearance: Adult bugs are ~2.5 mm long. Yellow immediately after moulting, turning brown to black with light grey-white wing markings after a few hours.
lifeCycle: Seven developmental stages: egg, five nymphal stages, and adult. At 25°C feeding on F. occidentalis, adults live 2–3 weeks and females lay ~50 eggs. Sex ratio is 50–60% females.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Embedded separately in plant tissue (leaf stem or main vein on leaf underside), difficult to see; colourless at first, turning milky-white.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Newly emerged nymphs are shiny and colourless, turning yellow after a few hours. N2 and N3 are yellowish-orange or brown; N4 and N5 are darker brown.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~2.5 mm long, brown to black with light grey-white spots.

conditions: Active >15°C (best >20°C, ~24–28°C; optimal population increase 28–29°C; high mortality at 15°C) at ~60% RH (~3 weeks / 15–20 d egg-to-adult at 21–25°C). Overwintering / Diapause: Adult females undergo reproductive diapause during winter induced by short daylength experienced by nymphs unless supplemental lighting is provided.

usage: Fairly good fliers that actively explore thrips-damaged leaves and flowers. Account for autumn short-day diapause if no supplemental lighting is used.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Native to East Asia; successfully used for biological control of thrips for over 10 years in Japan.
crops: Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predator with a strong preference for thrips, feeding on ALL plant-dwelling stages (larvae and adults), plus whiteflies, aphids, small caterpillars, mites, and pollen. Adult females eat ~20 Frankliniella occidentalis per day.
targets: All mobile stages of Thrips (Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci).
appearance: Adults are ~2 mm long, black with the leathery basal part of the wings yellowish-brown and the wing tips grey-white.
lifeCycle: Seven developmental stages: egg, five nymphal stages, and adult. When feeding on F. occidentalis at 25°C, adults live ~3 weeks and females lay ~125 eggs. Sex ratio is 50–60% females. Populations from Southern Japan do NOT undergo reproductive diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Embedded separately in plant tissue (leaf stem or main vein on leaf underside); newly laid egg is colourless and turns milky-white.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Shiny and colourless upon emergence, turning yellow after a few hours. N2 and N3 are yellowish-orange or brown; N4 and N5 have more extensive brown colouring.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~2 mm long; black body with yellowish-brown leathery wing bases and grey-white wing tips.

conditions: High mortality above 35°C.

usage: Actively explores plants and flowers; southern Japanese strains remain active without diapause.

taxonomy: Order Mesostigmata • Family Laelapidae (Soil Predatory Mite)
origin: Occurs naturally in Europe, North and South America, Asia, and Australia.
crops: Ornamentals, Seedlings, Vegetables, Bulbs, Greenhouse crops
effects: Soil-dwelling generalist predatory mite; nymphs and adults search for prey in the upper 1–2 cm of soil (larvae do not feed). Predates on sciarid fly (fungus gnat) eggs and larvae (adult females consume ~7 L1, 4 L2, 1.5 L3, or <1 L4 sciarid larvae/day), soil-dwelling thrips pre-pupae and pupae, shore fly larvae, springtails, mites, nematodes, and root mealybugs.
targets: Fungus gnat larvae (Bradysia spp.), Thrips pupae in the soil (Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci), and Shore fly larvae (Scatella tenuicosta).
appearance: Large mite with a body length of up to 1 mm. Body is pale with a clearly visible brown dorsal shield, brown legs, and brown mouthparts. Females are larger than males and have a distinctive white stripe on the rear end of the body.
lifeCycle: Passes through 5 stages: egg, six-legged non-feeding larva, eight-legged protonymph and deutonymph, and adult. Arrhenotokous (unfertilized females produce males; fertilized produce 50–70% females). Long lifespan: adult females survive 80 to 110 days at 20°C with food, and can survive 7 to 8 weeks without food! At 25°C, females lay ~2.4 eggs/day on sciarid larvae, ~0.8 eggs/day on F. occidentalis pre-pupae/pupae, or up to 3.4 eggs/day on mould mites (Tyrophagus putrescentiae).

stageBreakdown.Eggs: White, oval, and ~0.3 mm in length.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Eggs, six-legged non-feeding larvae, and first nymphal instars are white, with nymphs becoming light brown as they age.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Up to 1 mm long, pale body with brown dorsal shield, brown legs/mouthparts, and a white stripe on the rear end of females.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C) in moist, non-waterlogged upper growing-media layers. Juvenile development takes 35–45 days at 15°C and 12–13 days at 25°C. NO population growth at or below 10°C, and at 32°C egg mortality is very high with few eggs laid.

taxonomy: Order Mesostigmata • Family Macrochelidae (Soil Predatory Mite)
origin: Found in Europe, North and South America, Australia, and New Zealand; occurs in high numbers in greenhouse soils enriched with compost.
crops: Ornamentals, Bulbs, Seedlings, Vegetables, Greenhouse crops
effects: Fast-developing soil-dwelling generalist predatory mite; nymphs and adults feed on thrips pupae in the soil (adult females consume 4–5 F. occidentalis pupae/day), sciarid fly (fungus gnat) eggs and larvae, shore fly larvae, nematodes, mites, springtails, and other small soil organisms.
targets: Thrips pupae in the soil (F. occidentalis, T. tabaci), Fungus gnat eggs and larvae (Bradysia spp.), Shore fly larvae (Scatella tenuicosta), and Liriomyza pupae.
appearance: Adult mites are 0.6–0.8 mm long, oval-shaped, and pale white with a brown oval dorsal shield and brown legs. Females are larger than males and feature a white stripe on the rear end of the body.
lifeCycle: Passes through egg, six-legged larva, eight-legged protonymph and deutonymph, and adult. Note: Sometimes females produce larvae directly where the egg hatches inside the mother (larviparity). Arrhenotokous: unfertilized females produce only males, while fertilized females produce both males and females. Without food, adults can survive for 7 to 8 weeks.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Pearly white, oval, and about 0.3 x 0.2 mm in size (sometimes hatches inside mother via larviparity).
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Larvae are white (6 legs). Protonymphs and deutonymphs (8 legs) are pale white with a brown dorsal shield that becomes clearer with size.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 0.6–0.8 mm long, oval, pale white with brown oval dorsal shield and brown legs; females have a white stripe on rear.

conditions: Active >=15°C (best ~25°C) in moist, loose organic-rich substrates (~12–15 day population cycle in cool/standard media, accelerating to ~2 days egg-to-adult at 25°C on optimal prey). Fecundity peaks at 20–29°C (85–108 eggs/female). Low humidity reduces egg hatch, larval survival, and reproduction; oviposition begins at 13°C and stops above 33°C.

origin: Naturally occurring soil-dwelling entomopathogenic roundworm.
crops: Ornamentals, Seedlings, Vegetables, Mushrooms, Greenhouse crops
effects: Exhibits an intermediate foraging strategy combining ambushing and cruising traits (more cool-tolerant than many entomopathogenic nematodes). Infective juveniles enter the insect host and release symbiotic bacteria, killing thrips pupae, fungus gnat larvae, shore fly larvae, mushroom flies, leaf miners, and some caterpillars and weevils.
targets: Thrips pre-pupae and pupae in the soil (and foliar stages via spray), Sciarid fly / Fungus gnat larvae (Bradysia impatiens, Lycoriella spp.), Shore fly larvae (Scatella tenuicosta), Mushroom flies, Leaf miner larvae/pupae, and some caterpillars and weevils.
appearance: Microscopic unsegmented roundworms (infective juveniles).
lifeCycle: Because S. feltiae produces both male and female adults, at least two infective juvenile larvae (one male and one female) must invade a single target insect for the nematode population to reproduce inside the host. Populations in soil decline rapidly after application if hosts are scarce.
conditions: Active 10–31°C (best 14–26°C; effective across 8–33°C soil temperature). High soil moisture is essential; foliar applications require >75% RH for several hours and avoiding direct sunlight/UV.
usage: Application Guidelines: Used mainly as a soil drench against thrips pupae and fungus gnat larvae (or foliar spray against thrips/leaf miners). Apply late in the day at high humidity (>75% RH) with moist substrate at 10–31°C.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Mediterranean predatory phytoseiid mite used commercially across greenhouse sweet pepper, cucumber, aubergine, and ornamental crops.
crops: Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Aubergine, Ornamentals
effects: Mobile generalist phytoseiid mite that feeds on 1st and 2nd instar thrips larvae and small pest mites while readily multiplying on floral pollen when prey is absent.
targets: Thrips larvae (Frankliniella occidentalis, Thrips tabaci) and small pest mites.
appearance: Relatively large, dark brownish, oval-shaped phytoseiid predatory mite (~0.5 mm); easily visible against green leaves and white pepper flowers.
lifeCycle: Egg -> 6-legged larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; total cycle ~1–2 weeks depending on temperature. Establishes strongly where pollen is abundant.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval translucent eggs laid in leaf vein axils and flowers.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: 6-legged larva followed by active feeding 8-legged protonymph and deutonymph stages.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.5 mm shiny dark-brown oval mite, highly visible on leaves and petals.

conditions: Active ~7–40°C (best 20–28°C; inactive <7°C). Can tolerate low RH (critical RH ~30%); one of the most low-humidity-tolerant commercial predatory mites and remains active at high temperatures.
usage: Particularly effective in flowering sweet pepper during warm, dry greenhouse periods where humidity-sensitive mites struggle; castor bean or pepper pollen supports early establishment.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Biobest; Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Holarctic generalist phytoseiid mite adapted to both protected greenhouses and temperate outdoor berries, orchards, and woody nursery crops.
crops: Greenhouse crops, Berries, Strawberry, Raspberry, Apple, Fruit trees, Vineyards, Ornamentals, Woody crops
effects: Preventive generalist predatory mite feeding on spider mites, European red mites, thrips larvae, broad mites, cyclamen mites, and eriophyid russet mites, while persisting on pollen and fungal spores.
targets: Spider mites (Tetranychus urticae, Panonychus ulmi), Thrips larvae, Broad mites (Polyphagotarsonemus latus), Cyclamen mites (Phytonemus pallidus), and Rust/Russet mites (Aculops spp.).
appearance: Pale beige, pear-shaped phytoseiid mite (~0.4 mm).
lifeCycle: Egg -> larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; ~1–2 weeks. Generalist predator that survives on pollen, fungal spores, and alternative prey before spider mites arrive.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval whitish eggs deposited near leaf veins and hairs on leaf undersides.
stageBreakdown.Juveniles: 6-legged larva -> active 8-legged protonymph and deutonymph stages.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.4 mm pale beige pear-shaped mite.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C; also tolerates cooler spring/autumn conditions ~6–10°C and warm peaks up to 35°C). >=65% RH preferred; sensitive below 65% RH.
usage: Ideal early preventive sachet/broadcast release before summer heat or in cool-season outdoor berry and orchard canopies where P. persimilis cannot persist.
references: Biobest; Koppert Biological Systems; BC Ministry of Agriculture

origin: North American native phytoseiid mite; widely used outdoors and in protected berry, orchard, and ornamental crops in Canada and the US.
crops: Berries, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blueberry, Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Hop, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Fast-reproducing North American spider mite predator able to persist outdoors through temperate winters and respond rapidly to mite buildup on berries, hops, and fruit trees.
targets: Spider mites (Tetranychus urticae, European red mite, spruce spider mite) and broad/russet mites.
appearance: Small (~0.4 mm), translucent to reddish-orange pear-shaped predatory mite; eggs are oval and transparent.
lifeCycle: Egg (2–3 d) -> larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; ~7–10 days at 25°C.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval, transparent white eggs (2–3 d) laid on leaf undersides near mite colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Translucent to pale amber 6-legged larva and 8-legged protonymph/deutonymph.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.4 mm translucent to reddish-orange fast-moving pear-shaped mite.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best 15–25°C; tolerates cool outdoor conditions down to ~9°C). >70% RH preferred; requires >50% RH for good egg survival.
usage: Release at first sign of spider mites in strawberry, raspberry, blueberry, hop yards, and apple orchards; overwinters in ground cover and leaf litter in BC and temperate regions.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM

synonyms: Related species: Gaeolaelaps aculeifer (formerly Hypoaspis aculeifer)
taxonomy: Order Mesostigmata • Family Laelapidae (Soil Predatory Mite)
origin: Canadian native soil-dwelling predatory mite; performs exceptionally well in artificial greenhouse substrates (coco coir, rockwool, peat mixes).
crops: Greenhouse crops, Ornamentals, Vegetables, Bulbs, Seedlings, Mushrooms
effects: Substrate-dwelling predatory mite adapted to artificial greenhouse growing media (coco coir, rockwool, peat), hunting fungus gnat larvae, shore fly larvae, soil thrips pupae, and bulb mites.
targets: Fungus gnat larvae (Bradysia impatiens), Shore fly larvae (Scatella tenuicosta), Thrips pupae in substrate (Frankliniella occidentalis), and Bulb mites (Rhizoglyphus spp.).
appearance: Brown, relatively large soil-dwelling mite (~0.8–1.0 mm) with a sclerotized dorsal shield.
lifeCycle: Egg (2–3 d) -> 6-legged larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; ~18 days at 20°C.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: White oval eggs deposited in moist upper growing media (2–3 d).
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Whitish larva followed by pale-brown protonymph and deutonymph feeding on small substrate prey.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.8–1.0 mm brown mite with sclerotized dorsal shield.

conditions: Active 15–25°C (best 15–25°C; inactive around 14°C). Requires thoroughly moist (not flooded) substrate.
usage: Broadcast across coco coir, rockwool blocks, peat flats, and potting benches early in crop production; pairs well with Dalotia coriaria and Steinernema feltiae.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Cosmopolitan generalist foliar predator developed commercially in Canada for greenhouse and orchard biocontrol.
crops: Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Strawberry, Berries, Apple, Fruit trees, Cannabis, Ornamentals, Vegetables
effects: Large, hyper-active generalist foliar predator that runs rapidly across leaves and stems to capture aphids, both larval and adult thrips (including Echinothrips americanus), spider mites, and whiteflies.
targets: Aphids, Thrips (larvae and adults), Spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), Whiteflies, and Echinothrips americanus.
appearance: Large (1.0–1.5 mm), conspicuous bright red-orange mite with long legs; moves extremely fast in erratic, whirling ('whirligig') figure-eight patterns over foliage and flowers.
lifeCycle: Egg mass (9–30 d) -> prelarva -> 6-legged larva (8–9 d) -> 1st chrysalis (3–4 d) -> protonymph (2–3 d) -> 2nd chrysalis (3–4 d) -> deutonymph (4–6 d) -> 3rd chrysalis (2–3 d) -> tritonymph (3–4 d) -> 4th chrysalis (4–6 d) -> adult (lives 14–21 d, lays 45–150 eggs). Reproduces by parthenogenesis (all female). Active stages take ~3–4 weeks.

stageBreakdown.Eggs & Prelarva: Egg masses laid in secluded crevices (~9–30 d) followed by quiescent prelarva.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs (4 Chrysalis Molts): Free-living predatory larva, protonymph, deutonymph, and tritonymph separated by resting chrysalis stages (~3–4 weeks total).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 1.0–1.5 mm bright red-orange long-legged parthenogenetic females (live 14–21 d; lay 45–150 eggs).

conditions: Best ~24–25°C; ~60% RH optimum for development, with ~24°C and >70% RH recommended during initial establishment.
usage: Use especially for Echinothrips americanus and mixed thrips/aphid/spider mite hotspots on foliage where smaller phytoseiid mites struggle; avoid damaging fragile mites during release.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Western North American native predatory mite; prominent in perennial outdoor crops, orchards, vineyards, and dry/hot environments.
crops: Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Vineyards, Grapes, Berries, Strawberry, Hop, Nurseries
effects: Heat- and drought-adapted specialist spider mite predator capable of surviving at low prey densities and navigating spider mite webbing cleanly.
targets: Spider mites (Tetranychus urticae, Pacific spider mite, Willamette mite, European red mite) and russet mites.
appearance: Small (~0.36 mm), pear-shaped mite, translucent cream to red-brown depending on prey consumed.
lifeCycle: Egg -> 6-legged larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; ~6–12 days in warm conditions. Persists at low mite densities.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval translucent eggs deposited directly inside or near spider mite colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: 6-legged larva followed by active protonymph and deutonymph stages feeding on mite eggs and immatures.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.36 mm cream to red-brown pear-shaped predator.

conditions: Very broad thermal tolerance (~10–46°C reported depending on strain/crop; optimal 20–32°C). Tolerates dry conditions (~30–60% RH performs well; survival improved >=50% RH).
usage: Superior choice for hot, arid summer orchards, vineyards, and outdoor hops where P. persimilis fails from low humidity and heat stress.
references: UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Originates from southern Africa; prominent in the broader North American market for warm, dry greenhouse environments.
crops: Ornamentals, Rose, Tomato, Protected crops
effects: Warm- and dry-tolerant specialist spider mite predator with feeding speed similar to P. persimilis under lower-humidity greenhouse zones.
targets: Spider mites (Tetranychus urticae and Tetranychus cinnabarinus).
appearance: Small, pale/translucent to orange-red fast-moving phytoseiid mite resembling Phytoseiulus persimilis.
lifeCycle: Egg -> larva -> protonymph -> deutonymph -> adult; ~1 week in warm conditions.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval translucent eggs laid inside spider mite colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Nymphs: Fast-developing immature stages consuming spider mite eggs and juveniles.
stageBreakdown.Adults: Long-legged, fast-moving pale to orange-red predatory mite.

conditions: Active 12–32°C (best ~25°C; tolerates hotter, drier conditions than P. persimilis). Can function around 40–43% RH at ~21°C (requires higher RH as temperature rises).
usage: Deploy in upper greenhouse bench canopies, bright rose ranges, or dry interior zones where humidity drops below the threshold for Phytoseiulus persimilis.

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Anthocoridae (Minute Pirate Bug)
origin: Palearctic predatory flower bug; mainly used in European commercial greenhouse programs (not a major current Canadian commercial agent).
crops: Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Strawberry, Berries, Greenhouse vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Voracious anthocorid flower bug feeding on both larval and adult thrips as well as aphids, spider mites, whiteflies, and moth eggs; establishes even where pollen is limited.
targets: Thrips (larvae and adults), Aphids, Spider mites, Whiteflies, and Moth eggs.
appearance: 2.5–3 mm oval black predatory bug with white-grey wing patches; nymphs yellowish-orange to brown.
lifeCycle: Egg embedded in plant tissue -> 5 nymphal instars -> adult; ~21 days at 25°C. Can establish even in crops where pollen is limited.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Embedded singly in soft stem or main leaf vein tissue.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Wingless yellow-orange to brown predatory nymphs with red eyes.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2.5–3 mm black pirate bug with contrasting grey-white hemelytra patches.

conditions: Development 12–34°C (best 24–30°C) at ~60% RH. Enters reproductive diapause under short autumn/winter daylengths (<14–16h).
usage: In European protected cucumber and ornamentals where pollen is sparse, establishes earlier than some Orius species when pest prey is present.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Biobest; Koppert Biological Systems

taxonomy: Class Nematoda • Order Rhabditida • Family Heterorhabditidae
origin: Warm-temperature 'cruiser' entomopathogenic nematode; current commercial biological control agent in Canada.
crops: Berries, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blueberry, Cranberry, Turfgrass, Ornamentals, Nurseries, Container crops
effects: Classic warm-adapted cruiser entomopathogenic nematode: actively seeks sluggish subterranean beetle grubs and weevil larvae, enters via natural openings or rasps through intersegmental membranes with its dorsal tooth, and releases symbiotic Photorhabdus luminescens bacteria (REI: 0h).
targets: Black vine weevil (Otiorhynchus sulcatus) larvae/pupae, White grubs (Japanese beetle Popillia japonica, European chafer, June beetles), root weevils, and other soil-dwelling beetle larvae (REI: 0h).
appearance: Microscopic infective juvenile roundworms (~0.5–0.6 mm); possesses an anterior dorsal tooth used to rasp through thin intersegmental membranes of beetle grubs. Cadavers infected with H. bacteriophora turn characteristic brick-red / reddish-brown (and luminesce weakly in the dark) due to symbiotic Photorhabdus luminescens bacteria.
lifeCycle: Cruiser-type foraging: infective juveniles (IJs) actively swim through moist root-zone soil following CO2 and root-damage volatiles to locate sedentary grubs -> enter via natural openings or rasp through cuticle -> release symbiotic Photorhabdus luminescens bacteria -> host dies in 24–48h and turns red -> first generation is hermaphroditic (allowing a single IJ to reproduce inside a host) -> new IJs emerge in ~12–18 days.

stageBreakdown.Infective Juveniles (IJs): Soil-cruising 3rd-stage juveniles (~0.5–0.6 mm) with a dorsal cuticular tooth.
stageBreakdown.Infected Host Cadaver: Turns distinctive brick-red to reddish-brown within 48h from Photorhabdus luminescens.
stageBreakdown.Hermaphroditic Cycle: A single penetrating IJ matures into a self-fertile hermaphrodite inside the grub before subsequent bisexual generations.

conditions: Active 16–35°C (best 19–33°C; ineffective below ~12–15°C). Keep soil/media moist before and after application; avoid drying and direct UV sunlight.
usage: Drench late afternoon/cloudy days at warm soil temperatures (16–35°C) with pre- and post-application irrigation to move IJs into the root zone; inspect for diagnostic brick-red weevil/grub cadavers.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Aphidiinae (Endoparasitic Wasp)
origin: Native to Eurasia; widely introduced globally for biological control of large aphid species in greenhouses and field crops.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Potato, Strawberry, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary endoparasitoid roughly twice the size of Aphidius colemani that attacks larger aphid species not parasitized by A. colemani. Female drums host with antennae and injects an egg; developing larva turns the aphid into a swollen golden-brown mummy.
targets: Potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae) and Glasshouse potato aphid / Foxglove aphid (Aulacorthum solani).
appearance: Slender black wasps (~4–5 mm long), roughly twice the size of Aphidius colemani, more aggressive in pursuing prey, and darker at the waist. Forms large golden-yellow to golden-brown swollen mummies (~10–14 days after release).
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, 4 internal larval instars, pupa inside the mummified aphid cuticle, and adult wasp emerging through a round rear exit hole; first mummies appear ~10–14 days after release.
conditions: Optimal performance between 18°C and 25°C (best 20–25°C; efficacy declines above 28–30°C).
usage: Release preventively or at low initial densities of Macrosiphum euphorbiae and Aulacorthum solani; first mummies typically appear ~10–14 days after release. Often combined with Aphidius colemani and Aphelinus abdominalis.

taxonomy: Order Diptera • Family Cecidomyiidae (Predatory Aphid Gall Midge)
origin: Widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere; used commercially in greenhouses since the 1970s.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Melon, Aubergine, Strawberry, Rose, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals, Fruit trees
effects: Nocturnal gall midge where ONLY the larvae are predatory (small orange maggot with black mouthparts consuming 3–50+ aphids/day; adults are tiny slender mosquito-like midges feeding on honeydew that locate aphid colonies efficiently). Larvae paralyze aphids by injecting a neurotoxin into leg joints before sucking out body contents.
targets: Over 60 aphid species including Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, Macrosiphum euphorbiae, and Aulacorthum solani.
appearance: Adults are delicate, tiny slender mosquito-like long-legged midges (~2.5 mm) active at dusk/night. Predatory larvae are small bright orange maggots with black mouthparts (up to 2.5–3 mm) found feeding directly inside aphid colonies.
lifeCycle: Consists of oval orange eggs (laid in clusters among aphids), 3 predatory larval instars (lasting ~7–14 days), pupation in a cocoon in the upper soil layer (~10–14 days), and nocturnal adult midges.
conditions: Night temperatures >12°C required; best at 20–30°C (optimal 20–25°C) with >70% RH. Enters larval diapause in autumn when daylength drops below ~15.5 hours unless supplemental twilight lighting is used.
usage: Ideal for clearing established, high-density aphid colonies alongside parasitic wasps. Requires moist soil/substrate surface for pupation.

origin: Cosmopolitan across Europe, North America, and Asia.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Aubergine, Strawberry, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals, Fruit trees
effects: Voracious generalist predatory larvae ('aphid lions') that seize prey with sickle-shaped hollow mandibles, inject digestive enzymes, and suck out fluids. Consumes several hundred aphids during larval development, plus spider mites, thrips, whitefly larvae, mealybugs, and moth eggs.
targets: High-density hotspots of all aphid species (Myzus, Aphis, Macrosiphum, Aulacorthum), mealybugs, spider mites, thrips, whiteflies, psyllids, caterpillars, and moth eggs.
appearance: Adults are ~12–20 mm pale green with delicate net-veined wings and golden eyes (adults may turn brownish when overwintering and feed only on nectar, pollen, and honeydew). Larvae (2–10 mm) are grey/brown elongated alligator-like 'aphid lions' with large sickle-like jaws.
lifeCycle: Oval green eggs laid on slender silken stalks on leaves, 3 predatory larval instars, spherical white silken cocoon, and winged adult.
conditions: Active ~10–30°C (tolerates up to 35°C; best 20–28°C) and well suited to fluctuating or drier greenhouse humidities (better in drier air than Chrysoperla rufilabris).
usage: Introduce larvae directly into high-density aphid, caterpillar egg, or mealybug hotspots where sticky honeydew impairs parasitic wasps.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

synonyms: Related North American species: Diglyphus begini
origin: Native to Europe, North Africa, and Asia; introduced globally and used commercially since 1984. Often appears spontaneously in greenhouses and can overwinter outdoors in temperate regions.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Lettuce, Melon, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Celery, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary ECTOPARASITOID that parasitizes ALL Liriomyza species (L. bryoniae, L. trifolii, L. huidobrensis, L. sativae). Female paralyzes a 2nd or 3rd instar leaf miner larva and lays an egg beside it. Also kills substantial numbers of 1st and 2nd instar larvae via HOST FEEDING (puncturing larvae to feed on body fluids, which is required for wasp egg production). Supplants endoparasitoids like Dacnusa sibirica when both parasitize the same host.
targets: All Liriomyza leaf miners: L. bryoniae, L. trifolii, L. huidobrensis, and L. sativae.
appearance: Adults are 1.5–2.0 mm long, metallic green to black with short antennae. Females are larger with a broad black stripe over the hind leg; males have two small black bands. Presence in crop is signaled by short mines containing dead flattened larvae and pupation chambers with 6 black faecal pillars.
lifeCycle: All instars (egg, 3 larval instars, pupa, adult) develop OUTSIDE the host larva inside the leaf mine. Normally solitary, though at high densities two adults can occasionally develop from one large host larva.

stageBreakdown.Egg: Elongated, 0.3 x 0.1 mm, transparent white, laid alongside the paralyzed L2/L3 leaf miner larva.
stageBreakdown.Larva (3 Instars): Develop externally on the paralyzed host: L1 is colourless/transparent; L2 is yellow/semi-transparent with a brown fat body; L3 is blue-green. Older larvae leave the dead host and crawl back into the mine to pupate.
stageBreakdown.Pupa: Measures ~1.5 mm; starts green with red eyes, turning black. Lies between the upper and lower leaf epidermis held apart by SIX PILLARS made from larval faeces (which prevent the dried leaf epidermis from collapsing onto the pupa).
stageBreakdown.Adult: Metallic green/black with short antennae; escapes the mine by chewing a round hole through the upper epidermis (leaving round exit holes and black faecal spot pillars as diagnostic evidence).

conditions: 15–25°C best for balanced establishment; above 20–25°C, a population of D. isaea grows faster than either its leaf miner hosts or endoparasitoids (D. sibirica), providing superior control at higher temperatures and higher pest densities (below 20°C, Dacnusa sibirica often performs better).

usage: Introduce in spring/summer or when leaf miner densities and temperatures (>20°C) are rising. Supplied as adults in bottles (MIGLYPHUS).

synonyms: Related northern European species: Opius pallipes
taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Alysiinae (Endoparasitic Wasp)
origin: Native to Europe; introduced commercially since 1981. Appears spontaneously in greenhouses in all seasons and can overwinter inside leaf miner pupae.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Lettuce, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary ENDOPARASITOID that lays its eggs INSIDE first and second instar leaf miner larvae (does NOT perform host feeding). The parasitized leaf miner larva continues feeding and pupates normally in the soil, and the adult wasp later emerges from the host pupa.
targets: Liriomyza bryoniae and Liriomyza huidobrensis (less effective on L. trifolii; DOES NOT parasitize L. sativae).
appearance: Adults are black with brown legs, 2–3 mm long, with very long antennae consisting of at least 16 segments. External appearance of parasitized leaf miner larvae and pupae is unchanged (leaf dissection in a lab is required to detect internal eggs/larvae).
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, larva, pupa, and adult developing inside the host. Adults mate immediately after emerging; sex ratio is ~1:1 and adults live 1–3 weeks. If super-parasitization occurs (multiple eggs laid in one host), wasp larvae fight until only one survives.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Oval and clear white; injected inside L1 or L2 leaf miner larvae.
stageBreakdown.Larvae: Transparent with a small pointed head and small reddish-brown jaws; only moult for the first time and reach full development after the leaf miner host has pupated.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm, black with brown legs and long (>16-segment) antennae. Emerge from leaf miner pupae by biting a hole in the pupal cuticle with their jaws (oriented where the host's head was).

conditions: Especially effective at lower temperatures (<20°C, winter and spring) and low pest densities; performance declines as temperature rises (above 25°C, Diglyphus isaea is preferred). Minimum development time is 13 days at 27–30°C and ~30–32 days at 15°C. Highly efficient searcher using antennae and ovipositor to discriminate between parasitized and unparasitized hosts and visited vs. unvisited leaves.

usage: Recommended for winter and early spring when temperatures and leaf miner numbers are low, before transitioning to Diglyphus isaea as temperatures rise.

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Aphelinidae (Whitefly Parasitoid Wasp)
origin: Originates from a tropical/subtropical region; discovered in 1926 by an English tomato grower when black pupae of Trialeurodes vaporariorum emerged with wasps. Used commercially in greenhouses since 1972.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Poinsettia, Gerbera, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Endoparasitoid wasp that lays eggs inside L3 and L4 whitefly larvae (up to 150 eggs total; 5–15/day) and kills L2 larvae via HOST FEEDING (piercing with ovipositor to ingest body fluids). Highly skilled at discriminating and avoiding already-parasitized hosts (>90% accuracy).
targets: Greenhouse whitefly (Trialeurodes vaporariorum - optimal host) and Tobacco whitefly (Bemisia tabaci - less suitable host, used more for host feeding).
appearance: Adult female is ~0.6 mm long with a dark brown/black head and thorax and a bright yellow abdomen. Males are entirely black and hardly ever encountered (reproduction is 98%+ parthenogenetic/thelytokous).
lifeCycle: Consists of 6 stages (egg, 3 larval instars, pupa, adult), developing entirely inside the whitefly host. Unique in that its pupa forms immediately beneath and in contact with the whitefly pupal cuticle.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: 0.08 mm long and 0.03 mm wide; injected inside L3 or L4 whitefly scale.
stageBreakdown.Parasitized Pupa: Halfway through wasp development (~10 days), a parasitized T. vaporariorum pupa turns BLACK. When parasitizing B. tabaci, the pupa turns transparent brown rather than black.
stageBreakdown.Adult Exit: Full-grown wasp chews a round exit hole in the top of the host pupal cuticle, taking several hours to emerge.

conditions: Active ~18–30°C (operates most efficiently at 20–25°C; activity sharply reduced below ~18°C; development arrests below ~12°C and dies above ~38°C) and 50–80% RH (around 70% optimal). Egg-to-adult takes ~16–25 days depending on temperature. Short day length and low light intensity reduce flight and searching activity.

usage: Released on cards as parasitized black pupae (EN-STRIP). Combine with Eretmocerus eremicus (ENERMIX) when temperatures fluctuate or Bemisia tabaci is present.

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Superfamily Chalcidoidea • Family Aphelinidae
origin: Originates from the south-west of the United States; used commercially for biological control of whiteflies since 1994.
crops: Herbs, Poinsettia, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Greenhouse vegetables, Gerbera, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary ECTO-ENDOPARASITOID of both Bemisia tabaci and Trialeurodes vaporariorum: lays its egg outside BENEATH the L2/L3 whitefly larva, and upon hatching the wasp larva chews into the host. Also kills up to 30 whitefly larvae/day via HOST FEEDING (piercing the whitefly's excretory opening because its ovipositor is short).
targets: Tobacco/Silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci - highly effective) and Greenhouse whitefly (Trialeurodes vaporariorum).
appearance: Adult females (~0.75 mm) are lemon-yellow with green compound eyes, three red ocelli, and 5-segmented clubbed antennae; males are dark yellow to brown with 3-segmented antennae (enlarged terminal segment). Importantly, parasitized whitefly pupae turn translucent yellow/beige and do NOT turn black (unlike Encarsia formosa on T. vaporariorum).
lifeCycle: Population consists of ~60% females and 40% males (mating is required; unmated females produce only males). Total egg production is 50–200 eggs/female.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Pear-shaped, transparent, laid beneath L2 or L3 whitefly larva. Turns light brown after 2–3 days; egg remnants remain visible under the host as a brown circle. Egg does not hatch until the host reaches the L4 instar.
stageBreakdown.Parasitized Pupa: Host pupal cuticle turns an even, translucent yellow (does NOT turn black) with the developing adult wasp clearly visible inside.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 0.75 mm, lemon-yellow female with clubbed antennae and green eyes; emerges via a round exit hole gnawed in the pupal casing.

conditions: Active 20–30°C (best 25–30°C; maintains high activity at 30–40°C, outperforming Encarsia formosa at high heat) and 60–80% RH; also exhibits higher tolerance to synthetic chemical pesticides.

usage: Ideal for hot greenhouse conditions (30–40°C), poinsettia crops, and Bemisia tabaci infestations.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Miridae • Subfamily Dicyphinae
origin: Widely distributed in Europe, Northern Africa, and Western Asia; mainly used in European commercial greenhouse programs (whereas Dicyphus hesperus predominates in North America). Used commercially since 1994.
crops: Tomato, Aubergine, Solanaceous crops
effects: Generalist zoophytophagous predatory bug that moves effortlessly over sticky glandular hairs of tomato. Prefers whitefly eggs and larvae (adult consumes 30–40 whitefly eggs, 15–20 pupae, or 2–5 adults/day), and also eats 30–40 adult spider mites (T. urticae)/day, aphids, moth eggs (Tuta absoluta), small caterpillars, and leaf miner larvae.
targets: Whiteflies (T. vaporariorum, B. tabaci), Two-spotted spider mite hotspots (T. urticae), Leaf miner larvae (Liriomyza spp.), Aphids, and Moth eggs.
appearance: Slim green bugs with long legs and antennae: females 3.0–3.6 mm, males 2.9–3.1 mm. Diagnostic markings: first antennal segment is black, a black stripe runs behind the large brown compound eyes, and the basal forewing has a small black spot. Females have a large rounded abdomen with a visible ovipositor.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, 5 nymphal instars, and adult. Sex ratio is ~50% females, with males living longer than females. Mating occurs within 3 days of final moult; egg-laying starts 3 days later. Overwinters in the egg stage; nymphs can tolerate 6°C for a month. Populations can collapse in autumn due to Entomophthorales fungal infection.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Laid in older leaf veins, leaf stalks, and main stems (none laid in topmost 10–15 cm of young shoots). Invisible to naked eye; under microscope a minuscule pennant projects from the stem surface.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): N1 and N2 are yellow-green; older nymphs are green like adults with wing buds, but LACK the black first antennal segment and black eye stripe. Remain mostly on leaf undersides.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3.0–3.6 mm (females), green with black 1st antennal segment, black stripe behind eyes, and black forewing spot.

conditions: Temperatures >20°C preferred (development slows substantially <20°C; lower threshold 10–15°C and stops at 10°C; temperatures >40°C are lethal to nymphs; at 30°C only 42% of eggs hatch).

damage: Zoophytophagous Crop Risk: Requires plant sap to develop well, but cannot complete development on sap alone. If prey is scarce and bug populations exceed >100–150 per plant (especially during dull weather or in cherry/truss tomatoes and gerbera), feeding on plant sap causes flower abortion and fruit deformations during setting.
usage: Does not distinguish between unparasitized whitefly larvae and larvae recently parasitized by E. formosa, though hardened black (E. formosa) or yellow (E. eremicus) pupae are attacked less frequently.

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Miridae • Subfamily Dicyphinae
origin: Distributed worldwide; widely used in Mediterranean greenhouse tomato production since 2003 (import/release restricted in some northern countries due to zoophytophagous plant damage risks).
crops: Tomato, Aubergine
effects: Aggressive generalist zoophytophagous predator feeding on whiteflies (prefers eggs and larvae), Tuta absoluta moth eggs (adults eat >30 Tuta eggs/day!), spider mites, aphids, small caterpillars, and leaf miner larvae.
targets: Whiteflies (B. tabaci, T. vaporariorum), Tomato leaf miner moth (Tuta absoluta eggs), Spider mites, Aphids, and Leaf miners.
appearance: Adults are 3–4 mm long with a slim build, long legs, and antennae. Green with grey-black markings: ALL antennal segments are grey-black, a black mark sits between the large red-brown compound eyes, and there is a black collar behind the head.
lifeCycle: Consists of egg, 5 nymphal instars, and adult (~50% females). Females lay ~5 eggs/day at 22°C (60–80 eggs over first 3 weeks at 20–35°C). Cannot enter diapause and is NOT sensitive to the Entomophthorales fungus that collapses M. pygmaeus.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Laid in older leaf veins, leaf/fruit stalks, and main stems (tiny pennant projects from surface under microscope).
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): N1 and N2 are yellow-green; older nymphs are green with grey-black antennal bases and visible wing buds.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3–4 mm long, green with completely grey-black antennae, black mark between eyes, and black pronotal collar.

conditions: Optimum temperature range is 20–30°C (tolerates high Mediterranean heat better than M. pygmaeus). Constant temperatures >40°C are lethal; at 5°C nymphs die within 22 days, and at 15°C only 52% survive to adulthood.

damage: Zoophytophagous 'Necrotic Ring' Damage: Nymphs cannot complete development on plant sap alone. taxonomy: Order Coleoptera • Family Coccinellidae • Subfamily Sticholotidinae (Predatory Ladybeetle)
origin: Originates from Central America.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Poinsettia, Gerbera, Hibiscus, Ornamentals
effects: Specialized whitefly predator: both adults and larvae feed EXCLUSIVELY on whiteflies (T. vaporariorum and B. tabaci) with a strong preference for eggs. A larva consumes almost 1,000 whitefly eggs to complete development, and an adult consumes up to 160 whitefly eggs/day (or 12 L4 larvae/day).
targets: Whitefly hotspots (Trialeurodes vaporariorum and Bemisia tabaci eggs and larvae).
appearance: Tiny (1–2 mm), hemispherical, shiny black/dark brown lady beetle with short antennae and biting mouthparts (female head dark brown; male head light brown). Larvae are cream/yellow-white, elongated and hairy (growing up to 4 mm). Yellow faecal spots on leaves indicate colonies.
lifeCycle: Egg (4–5 d) -> 4 larval instars (8–12 d) -> pupa (5–6 d) -> adult (~50% females; females live up to 138 days in lab). Females ONLY lay eggs when consuming 100–150 whitefly eggs/day (laying ~9 eggs/day at 22°C, up to 544 eggs on B. tabaci at 26°C). Does NOT enter diapause.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Approx. 0.5 mm, oval, white (4–5 d); laid singly on leaf undersides inside whitefly colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): Cream/yellow-white, elongated and hairy with small dark dots (8–12 d), reaching 4 mm when full-grown.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: Attach via abdomen along leaf veins on lower leaves (5–6 d); roundish, white, covered with short white hairs.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 1–2 mm shiny black/dark brown lady beetle; drops and plays dead when disturbed.

conditions: Active 15–35°C (best 25–30°C; development ~16–20 days; adults do not fly <13°C; larvae die at constant <15°C or >35°C). Optimal RH ~75–85% (immature survival reduced <50% RH).
