usage: Curative hotspot treatment: Because D. catalinae searches by touch rather than scent and requires high prey density (100–150 eggs/day), beetles die off if food runs out rather than dispersing.

synonyms: Aphidius colemani, Aphidius matricariae, Aphidius ervi, Praon volucre, Ephedrus cerasicola, Aphelinus abdominalis, Adalia bipunctata, Hippodamia convergens, Coleomegilla maculata, Didion longulum, Aphidoletes aphidimyza, Eupeodes americanus, Chrysoperla carnea, Chrysoperla rufilabris, Micromus variegatus, Hemerobius spp.
origin: Used globally in integrated greenhouse and field aphid management.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Melon, Aubergine, Strawberry, Herbs, Chrysanthemum, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Host-specific parasitic wasps (Aphidius colemani, A. matricariae, A. ervi, Praon volucre, Ephedrus cerasicola, Aphelinus abdominalis) locate and parasitize aphids at low initial densities, whereas generalist predators (Aphidoletes aphidimyza gall midge, Eupeodes americanus hoverfly, Adalia bipunctata, Hippodamia convergens, Coleomegilla maculata & Didion longulum lady beetles, Chrysoperla & Micromus lacewings, Dicyphus hesperus, Nabis americoferus, and Anystis baccarum) clear high-density aphid colonies rapidly.
targets: Aphid species: Aphidius colemani targets Aphis and Myzus spp.; A. matricariae targets Myzus persicae (NOT Aphis gossypii); A. ervi and Aphelinus abdominalis target Macrosiphum euphorbiae and Aulacorthum solani; generalist predators consume all aphid species.
appearance: Parasitic wasps convert aphids into swollen golden-brown or black leathery 'mummies' (or a silky pedestal beneath the aphid in Praon volucre).
lifeCycle: Parasitoids develop inside the aphid host; predators consume hundreds to thousands of aphids across larval and adult stages.
conditions: Parasitoid efficacy can be impaired by hyperparasitoids in summer; cool-adapted predators (Micromus variegatus, Eupeodes americanus) sustain suppression below 15°C.
usage: Release specific parasitic wasps preventively or at the very beginning of an aphid infestation, and introduce generalist predators into established hotspots.

synonyms: Closely related species complex: Aphidius transcaspicus
taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Aphidiinae (Aphid Endoparasitoid Wasp)
origin: Presumed to be of Indian origin; now naturalized worldwide and widely used for biological control of aphids.
crops: Herbs, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Melon, Aubergine, Tomato, Greenhouse vegetables, Strawberry, Chrysanthemum, Rose, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary endoparasitoid with highly effective searching behaviour that tracks down aphids even at low densities. Female drums the aphid with her antennae to verify species and unparasitized status, stands on outstretched legs, bends her abdomen forward beneath her thorax between her legs, and pierces the aphid to deposit an egg in <0.5 seconds. Wasp presence triggers aphid alarm pheromone release, causing aphids to drop from leaves.
targets: Cotton aphid (Aphis gossypii), Peach potato aphid (Myzus persicae subsp. persicae), and Tobacco aphid (Myzus persicae subsp. nicotianae). Does not parasitize Macrosiphum euphorbiae or Aulacorthum solani.
appearance: Slender black wasps (~2–3 mm; half the size of A. ervi and lighter at the waist). Females have a pointed abdomen as long as their wings with an ovipositor and light brown legs; males have slightly longer antennae, a rounded abdomen shorter than their wings, and dark brown legs. Parasitized aphids swell into golden-yellow or golden-brown mummies.
lifeCycle: Mating occurs within 1 day of emergence (females mate once; males mate multiple times). Sex ratio is ~2:1 (female:male). A single female can lay >300 eggs, mostly during the first 3 days after emergence. Four larval instars develop inside the aphid; 2nd and 3rd instar aphids are preferred (parasitized L4/adults reproduce for 2 more days; younger parasitized nymphs produce 0 offspring).

stageBreakdown.Oviposition & Larvae (4 Instars): Injected in <0.5 seconds; 4 larval instars feed internally while the aphid continues feeding and secreting honeydew for several days.
stageBreakdown.Mummy Stage: After 7–12 days (temperature-dependent), the full-grown larva spins a cocoon inside the aphid cuticle, swelling and hardening it into a golden-yellow to golden-brown mummy.
stageBreakdown.Adult Emergence: 4–6 days after mummification, the adult wasp emerges by chewing a round exit hole in the mummy. Avoids entering very dense, sticky honeydew-covered colonies.

conditions: Best at 20–25°C (development ~15 days at 20°C; activity reduced above 30°C). Adult lifespan is ~10 days at 18–22°C, and summer population growth can be hindered by hyperparasitoids.

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Aphidiinae
origin: European origin; occurs widely in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, North America, Peru, and Brazil.
crops: Herbs, Sweet pepper, Tomato, Aubergine, Strawberry, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Solitary endoparasitoid specific to aphids of the family Aphididae (genera Myzus, Aphis, Ovatus, Rhopalosiphum, and Sitobion). Biology closely resembles Aphidius colemani, turning parasitized aphids into golden-brown mummies.
targets: Used in greenhouses primarily against Myzus species (Myzus persicae). Note: Does NOT target Aphis gossypii.
appearance: Adults are 3–4 mm golden-brown wasps with long antennae. Key distinguishing feature: presence of fine stripes on the side parts of the wasp's waist.
lifeCycle: Closely resembles Aphidius colemani: internal larval development followed by pupation inside a swollen golden-brown aphid mummy and emergence through a round rear exit hole.
conditions: Best at 15–25°C (optimal 20–25°C; activity reduced above 28°C or below 15°C) and ~60–80% RH. Better adapted to cooler greenhouse temperatures than Aphidius colemani.
usage: Ideal for controlling Myzus persicae in cooler greenhouse regimes where it outperforms A. colemani.

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Superfamily Chalcidoidea • Family Aphelinidae
origin: Used commercially in greenhouses since 1993 and in cereal banker plant systems.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Potato, Strawberry, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Endoparasitoid of Macrosiphum, Aulacorthum, and Myzus species (with a strong preference for Macrosiphum euphorbiae) and Sitobion avenae in banker plants. Achieves control via parasitization and HOST FEEDING in roughly equal measure: pierces small aphid nymphs with its ovipositor and sucks them empty without laying an egg, while parasitizing larger (preferred L3) instars and even winged adults.
targets: Potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae), Glasshouse potato aphid (Aulacorthum solani), Myzus spp., and grain aphid (Sitobion avenae) on banker plants.
appearance: Adults are 2.5–3 mm long with short legs and short antennae; females have a black thorax and yellow abdomen, while males are slightly smaller with a darker abdomen. Prefer walking over flying and jump when disturbed. Parasitized aphids harden into leathery, BLACK, elongated (less swollen than Aphidius) mummies where antennae and cornicles remain recognizable.
lifeCycle: Egg inside aphid (~2–3 d) -> internal larva (~7 d) -> black leathery mummy/pupa (~8 d) -> adult (~16–18 d total at ~20–24°C). Sex ratio 1:1. After examining an aphid with antennal tips, female curls wing tips and inserts long ovipositor for several minutes. Adult lives several weeks (~30 d), deposits 5–10 eggs/day in juvenile aphids (~250 eggs total), and also host-feeds. Less affected by Asaphes hyperparasitoids in practice than Aphidius spp.

stageBreakdown.Oviposition & Host Feeding: Female inserts ovipositor for several minutes to lay an egg in larger (L3) aphids, or pierces and drains small nymphs via host feeding.
stageBreakdown.Black Mummy: First mummies turn leathery and black 7 days after parasitization (at 24°C); more elongated and less swollen than Aphidius mummies.
stageBreakdown.Adult Exit: Adult emerges after ~16–18 days total (16 d at 24°C) through an irregularly serrated hole at the posterior end of the black mummy.

conditions: Active 15–35°C (performs relatively well at >28°C compared to Aphidius spp.; no specific commercial RH threshold published). Development from egg to adult takes ~16 days at 24°C; stays in the crop longer (~30-day lifespan) and migrates more slowly.

~30 days (Withstands high temperatures >28°C better than Aphidius spp.)

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Aphidiinae
origin: One of the most abundant naturally occurring parasitoids of aphids in Europe; released in Chile in the 1970s on wheat (against Metopolophium dirhodum and Sitobion avenae) and now established on a wide range of hosts.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Aubergine, Strawberry, Rose, Cereals, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Endoparasitoid of many aphid species, especially effective against the potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae).
targets: Potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae), Aulacorthum solani, Myzus persicae, Metopolophium dirhodum, and Sitobion avenae.
appearance: Diagnostic Pupation Pedestal: Unlike Aphidius or Ephedrus which pupate inside the aphid skin, the full-grown Praon volucre larva leaves the hollowed aphid cuticle and pupates UNDER the aphid, spinning a characteristic silky, whitish, transparent tent-like pedestal beneath the empty aphid skin.
lifeCycle: Female lays an egg inside the aphid where the larva develops before emerging underneath to spin its silky cocoon pedestal. At 22°C, females can lay up to 500 eggs in Macrosiphum euphorbiae over an 18-day period (with 50% of eggs laid during the first 5 days). Adult emerges through a round hole.
conditions: Parasitism is optimal between 16°C and 22°C. Wasps are inactive below 15°C, and adult longevity decreases strongly at 25°C. Oviposition-to-adult development takes 26 days at 16°C and 13 days at 23–25°C.

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Aphidiinae
origin: Occurs naturally throughout Europe.
crops: Sweet pepper, Paprika, Tomato, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Endoparasitoid of greenhouse aphids (such as Myzus persicae). Developing larva spins an internal cocoon, causing the parasitized aphid to swell and harden into a leathery, black, rounded mummy.
targets: Peach potato aphid (Myzus persicae) and related greenhouse aphids.
appearance: Adult wasps are black and measure ~4–5 mm in length. Mummies are leathery and black, more rounded than Aphelinus abdominalis mummies, and display a distinctive silvery underside when detached from the leaf. Adult emerges through a round hole at the rear of the mummy.
lifeCycle: Females mate only once, but oviposit throughout most of their adult life. Mummies are found on the plant as well as in hidden locations such as on crop ropes or under pot rims.
conditions: Optimal temperature for population development is 20–25°C; mummies show high tolerance to low temperatures. In Myzus persicae on sweet pepper/paprika, egg-to-adult development takes 33.7 days at 15°C, ~21 days at 21°C, and 19 days at 24°C. Adult lifespan ranges from 26.2 days at 15°C down to 2.8 days at 32°C.

usage: Check both plant foliage and concealed structures (ropes, pot rims) for rounded black mummies with a silvery ventral base.

origin: Occurs naturally throughout Europe, Central Asia, and North America; released commercially for biological control of aphids in greenhouses and woody crops.
crops: Orchards, Shrubs, Trees, Greenhouse vegetables, Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Fruit trees, Soft fruits, Rose, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Generalist predator: both adults and larvae predate on ALL species of aphids (an adult consumes several thousand aphids in its lifetime; 4th-instar larvae consume as many aphids per day as adults), plus psyllids, mealybugs, scales, spider mites, and lepidopteran eggs. Search behaviour shifts from rapid/superficial to slow/intensive once an aphid colony is encountered.
targets: Mainly aphids (Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, Macrosiphum euphorbiae, Aulacorthum solani); also psyllids (Bactericera cockerelli), mealybugs (Planococcus citri), scales, spider mites, and lepidopteran eggs.
appearance: Adults are 3.5–5.5 mm long (males smaller than females); head and thorax are mainly black with small white markings; bright red to orange-yellow elytra (wing cases) each with a single black spot (melanic black forms with red spots also occur). Larvae grow to 5–6 mm and are brown or blackish-grey with black and yellow/orange spots.
lifeCycle: Females lay up to 1,500 eggs in small batches (10–50 eggs, averaging ~20 eggs/day) on leaf undersides close to aphid colonies. Larval emergence takes 4–8 days, and egg-to-adult development takes ~16 days at 25°C. Adults live up to 3 months and hibernate over winter in sheltered refugia.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: 1.0–1.5 mm long, orange-yellow, laid in batches of 10–50 on leaf undersides near aphid colonies (hatch in 4–8 days).
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): Brown or blackish-grey with black and yellow/orange spots, reaching 5–6 mm; L4 larvae match adult daily aphid consumption.
stageBreakdown.Pupae: 3.0–3.5 mm long, dark grey to black with yellow dots, hanging attached to leaves.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3.5–5.5 mm red/orange ladybird with two black spots (or black with red spots); live up to 3 months.

conditions: Active 13–35°C (best 24–28°C) and 30–90% RH (best 70–80% RH). Requires high aphid density to retain adults; in sunny conditions, adult ladybirds tend to fly out of greenhouse vents.
usage: Release larvae (rather than flying adults) directly into concentrated, high-density aphid hotspots.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems

taxonomy: Order Heteroptera • Family Miridae • Subfamily Dicyphinae
origin: North American native zoophytophagous mirid bug; major Canadian commercial biological control agent for greenhouse tomato, pepper, and cucumber.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Mullein, Ornamentals, Greenhouse vegetables
effects: Voracious North American mirid predator well adapted to glandular trichomes of tomato stems and leaves; pierces whitefly eggs and larvae, thrips, aphids, spider mites, psyllids, moth eggs, and small caterpillars.
targets: Whiteflies (Trialeurodes vaporariorum, Bemisia tabaci), Thrips (Frankliniella occidentalis), Aphids, Spider mites, Psyllids (Bactericera cockerelli), Moth eggs, and small caterpillars.
appearance: Adult ~6 mm long, slender green/black mirid bug with long legs, dark pronotum/wings, and large bright red eyes; nymphs are green and wingless.
lifeCycle: Egg inserted into plant tissue -> 5 nymphal instars -> adult; takes ~5 weeks (35 d) at 25°C and ~8 weeks (56 d) at 20°C. Often established early in greenhouse tomatoes using common mullein (Verbascum thapsus) banker plants.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Elongate eggs embedded inside plant stems and main leaf veins.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Wingless bright-green active nymphs with red eyes and growing wing pads.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~6 mm slender green-and-black long-legged mirid bug with bright red eyes.

conditions: Active >15°C (best 20–35°C) at >=60% RH.
damage: Zoophytophagous: like Macrolophus pygmaeus and Nesidiocoris tenuis, D. hesperus feeds on plant sap as well as prey and may feed on plants or blemish fruit when prey is scarce or bug populations are high.
usage: Pre-establish on common mullein (Verbascum thapsus) banker plants or early tomato crops before heavy whitefly pressure arrives; supplement with Ephestia kuehniella eggs during low-prey phases.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

synonyms: Common damsel bug, Pale damsel bug
origin: North American native generalist predator; commercially available in Canada for greenhouse and field biological control.
crops: Vegetables, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Strawberry, Berries, Alfalfa, Field crops, Ornamentals
effects: Fast-moving generalist ambush predator that uses raptorial forelegs to seize soft-bodied pests, moth eggs, thrips, aphids, whiteflies, and lygus bugs before draining them through its curved piercing beak.
targets: Aphids, Thrips, Whiteflies, Spider mites, Lygus bugs, Leafhoppers, and small caterpillars/moth eggs.
appearance: 10–13 mm slender tan to greyish-brown bug with enlarged raptorial front legs for seizing prey and a curved piercing beak.
lifeCycle: Egg inserted into plant stems -> 5 nymphal instars -> adult; complete cycle ~7–10 weeks depending on temperature.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Deposited into soft plant stems with a flat white cap flush at the stem surface.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): Wingless slender tan nymphs mimicking fast-moving ants or slender bugs.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 10–13 mm elongate pale tan/greyish-brown damsel bug with raptorial front legs.

conditions: Best 20–28°C and 50–70% RH.
usage: Release in protected vegetable/strawberry crops or conserve grassy and flowering field margins where adults shelter and forage.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM

taxonomy: Order Hemiptera • Family Pentatomidae • Subfamily Asopinae
origin: North American native predatory stink bug; commercially reared in Canada and the US.
crops: Tomato, Potato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Brassica, Cabbage, Corn, Berries, Orchards, Field crops, Greenhouse vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Voracious generalist stink bug predator targeting >90 insect prey species, including large exposed caterpillars and defoliating beetle larvae. Injects potent paralyzing venom through a thick predatory beak.
targets: Caterpillars (cabbage looper, armyworms, hornworms, diamondback moth) and beetle larvae (Colorado potato beetle, Mexican bean beetle); >90 insect prey species.
appearance: Adult ~11–13 mm brown shield-shaped stink bug distinguished from the pest Brown Marmorated Stink Bug (Halyomorpha halys) by having sharp, pointed shoulder (humeral) spines, uniform brown antennae (NO white bands), a less strongly banded abdomen edge, and a short, thick, robust predatory beak (rostrum). Early nymphs are red and black; older nymphs have cream, red, and black abdominal markings.
lifeCycle: Barrel-shaped metallic eggs laid in clusters -> 5 nymphal instars -> adult (~25–35 days at 25°C). May occasionally probe plants for moisture, but is strictly beneficial.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Barrel-shaped bronze/metallic eggs crowned with slender hair-like spines, laid in tight foliar clusters.
stageBreakdown.Nymphs (5 Instars): 1st instars take plant moisture only; 2nd–5th instars are brightly patterned red/black/cream active predators.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 11–13 mm mottled tan-brown stink bug with sharp pointed shoulder spines, unbanded brown antennae, and short thick beak.

conditions: Active mainly >15°C (best 20–30°C) at 50–70% RH. Below ~15°C combined with short daylength, reproductive diapause can occur.

crops: Strawberry, Berries, Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Lettuce, Herbs, Cool-season crops, Greenhouse vegetables, Ornamentals

Adults often fly away unless floral nectar/honeydew is present
Adults remain hunting in aphid colonies because they eat prey directly

usage: Top choice for early-season or unheated greenhouses, lettuce, herbs, and strawberries when temperatures drop below 15°C and parasitic wasps slow down.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems

origin: Naturally occurring beneficial brown lacewings in North American forests, orchards, and field crops (natural BCA; not currently commercially produced).
crops: Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Shrubs, Trees, Berries, Field crops
effects: Naturally occurring cool-season brown lacewings in BC orchards, conifers, and field edges where both adults and larvae consume aphids, psyllids, mealybugs, mites, and caterpillars.
targets: Aphids, Mealybugs, Psyllids, Thrips, Mites, Whiteflies, small caterpillars, and insect eggs.
appearance: Adult ~5–10 mm, soft-bodied brown lacewing with hairy net-veined wings held roof-like over the body; larva flattened and alligator-like.
lifeCycle: Eggs laid singly without a stalk (H. stigma eggs ~11 d) -> 3 larval instars -> silken cocoon/pupa (~9–14 d) -> adult; many species have ~2 generations/year. Both adults and larvae are predatory.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Unstalked oval eggs deposited singly on foliage, needles, or twigs (H. stigma ~11 d).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 5–10 mm mottled brown predatory lacewings active even in crisp spring/fall weather.

conditions: Notably cold-tolerant; often active in cooler spring and fall conditions.
usage: Conserve naturally occurring Hemerobius populations in orchards, shelterbelts, and nursery stock by avoiding broad-spectrum dormant or spring insecticides.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Anatis Bioprotection; UC IPM

origin: North American native hoverfly; commercially available in Canada for greenhouse and field aphid biological control.
crops: Sweet pepper, Tomato, Cucumber, Strawberry, Berries, Lettuce, Brassicas, Greenhouse vegetables, Field crops, Ornamentals
effects: Voracious aphid-hunting maggot combined with a strong-flying pollinating adult: females pinpoint sparse aphid colonies at cool temperatures and lay eggs right beside them, while larvae consume hundreds of aphids.
targets: Aphids (Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, Macrosiphum euphorbiae, Aulacorthum solani, and other aphid species).
appearance: Adult is a wasp-mimicking black-and-yellow striped hoverfly with large reddish-brown eyes; larva is a legless, slug-like green/brown/tan maggot.
lifeCycle: Single white egg laid near aphid colony -> 3 predatory larval instars (voraciously preying on aphids) -> teardrop-shaped brown puparium -> nectar/pollen-feeding adult hoverfly that also acts as a crop pollinator.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Chalky white oblong eggs with textured sculptured shell placed singly beside aphid colonies.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (3 Instars): Blind legless green/brown/tan tapering maggots that rear up to probe and drain aphids.
stageBreakdown.Pupae & Adults: Teardrop-shaped puparium on foliage/soil -> black-and-yellow wasp-mimic fly feeding on pollen and nectar.

conditions: Best activity ~10–25°C; remains active and searches for aphid colonies at relatively low temperatures where other predators slow down. Flowering companion resources (e.g., Sweet Alyssum) support adult longevity and egg-laying.
usage: Release pupae in cool-to-moderate greenhouse vegetables or berries alongside nectar/pollen companion strips (such as Sweet Alyssum, Lobularia maritima) to maximize adult oviposition.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; Biobest; BC Ministry of Agriculture

origin: One of the best-known and most common native North American lady beetles, occurring from southern Canada through much of the Americas.
crops: Vegetables, Alfalfa, Cereals, Wheat, Apple, Orchards, Strawberry, Berries, Field crops, Greenhouse crops, Ornamentals
effects: Classic native generalist lady beetle where both adults and alligator-like larvae consume dozens of aphids per day alongside small soft-bodied insects, scales, mites, and insect eggs.
targets: Mainly aphids; also small soft-bodied insects, insect eggs, scales, and mites.
appearance: Adult 4–7 mm; orange-red wing covers (elytra) typically with black spots; black pronotum (thorax shield) bordered in white with two characteristic CONVERGING white dashes/marks. Larva (up to 10 mm in L4) is dark alligator-like with orange-yellow spots on abdominal segments.
lifeCycle: Yellow spindle-shaped eggs laid in upright clusters -> 4 predatory larval instars -> orange-and-black hemispherical pupa -> predatory adult.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Upright clusters of 10–30 bright yellow spindle-shaped eggs on leaf undersides.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): Up to 10 mm dark grey/black alligator-like larvae with bright orange abdominal patches.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 4–7 mm orange-red beetle with 0–13 black spots and diagnostic converging white dashes on a black thorax.

conditions: Active 12–25°C (best ~29°C) at ~50–70% RH. Highly mobile; field-collected adults may disperse rapidly after release unless pre-conditioned or released into dense aphid colonies.
usage: Release late in the evening at the base of aphid-infested plants with misted foliage, or choose insectary-reared/pre-conditioned stock to minimize immediate migratory dispersal.
references: UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems

synonyms: Pink spotted lady beetle, Twelve-spotted lady beetle
origin: Native North American generalist lady beetle used in Canadian and US biological control programs.
crops: Corn, Sweet corn, Potato, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Cabbage, Brassicas, Alfalfa, Berries, Field crops, Greenhouse crops, Ornamentals
effects: Pollen-assisted native generalist lady beetle that consumes aphids, spider mites, thrips, and eggs of major caterpillar and beetle pests (corn borer, cabbage looper, fall armyworm, Colorado potato beetle) while persisting on pollen when prey is scarce.
targets: Aphids, Insect eggs (including European corn borer, Colorado potato beetle, cabbage looper, fall armyworm), Spider mites, Thrips, and other soft-bodied prey.
appearance: Adult 5–7 mm, elongate-oval, pink-red to orange with 12 large black spots (6 on each wing cover) and two large black triangles on the pink/orange pronotum.
lifeCycle: Egg cluster -> 4 predatory larval instars -> pupa -> adult. Generalist omnivore: adults and larvae can complete development on plant pollen (up to 50% of diet) when insect prey is scarce.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Clusters of pale yellow oval eggs laid on foliage near prey or pollen sources.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): Elongate dark grey/black alligator-like larvae with yellow/pink dorsal markings.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 5–7 mm elongate pink-red beetle with 12 black elytral spots and two black pronotal triangles.

conditions: Active >15°C (best 18–30°C) at 50–70% RH.
usage: Ideal in pollen-producing row and greenhouse crops (corn, pepper, brassicas, potatoes) where pollen reserves stabilize populations between pest outbreaks.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture

taxonomy: Order Coleoptera • Family Coccinellidae • Subfamily Scymninae
origin: Native North American lady beetle (naturally associated with deciduous trees) and currently commercially available in Canada.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Ornamentals, Deciduous trees, Greenhouse vegetables
effects: Tiny native coccinellid predator able to forage into tight growing points and sticky aphid colonies; both waxy mealybug-like larvae and adults actively consume aphids and other small soft-bodied insects.
targets: Many aphid species (Myzus persicae, Aphis gossypii, Macrosiphum euphorbiae, Aulacorthum solani) and other small soft-bodied insects.
appearance: Very small (1.4–1.8 mm), elongate-oval, finely hairy dark brown-to-black beetle with a brown/reddish-brown head. Larvae are covered in conspicuous white waxy filaments resembling mealybugs, but are fast-moving voracious aphid predators.
lifeCycle: Egg (3–5 d) -> 4 wax-covered predatory larval instars (2–3 wk) -> pupa (3–5 d) -> predatory adult (lives several months); complete cycle typically ~3–4 weeks. Both larvae and adults are predatory.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Minute yellow eggs hidden near aphid colonies (3–5 d).
stageBreakdown.Waxy Larvae (4 Instars): Conspicuously covered in white waxy tufts (frequently mistaken for mealybugs! Move rapidly to devour aphids).
stageBreakdown.Adults: Tiny (1.4–1.8 mm) hairy dark-brown/black beetle with reddish-brown head living several months.

conditions: Active >15°C (best 20–25°C) at 50–70% RH (best ~60% RH).
usage: Release directly into greenhouse tomato, cucumber, and pepper aphid hotspots; alert staff not to mistake its beneficial white waxy larvae for mealybug pests.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture

metabolite: Multicolored Asian Lady Beetle (Harmonia axyridis — Invasive)
synonyms: Multicolored Asian lady beetle, Harlequin ladybird, Asian lady beetle
origin: Native to eastern Asia; historically introduced to North America and Europe for biological control of aphids, but now an invasive nuisance species across British Columbia and North America and NOT recommended for intentional release in Canada.
crops: Apple, Orchards, Vineyards, Grapes, Berries, Field crops, Shrubs, Trees
effects: Historically released for aphid control, now recognized as an aggressive intraguild predator and agricultural/domestic nuisance: displaces native lady beetles, bites people, aggregates inside buildings in autumn, and taints crushed wine grapes with alkylmethoxypyrazine.
targets: Preys on aphids and soft-bodied insects, but outcompetes native lady beetles (Hippodamia convergens, Adalia bipunctata, Coccinella spp.), aggregates inside buildings in autumn, bites humans, and contaminates wine grapes with alkylmethoxypyrazine defensive alkaloids.
appearance: Large (6–10 mm), dome-shaped beetle with highly variable yellow, orange, red, or black elytra (0 to 19+ spots, or black with red spots). Diagnostic mark: a black 'M'- or 'W'-shaped marking on the pale white/cream pronotum.
lifeCycle: Clustered yellow eggs -> spiny black-and-orange 4-instar larvae -> pupa -> overwintering aggregating adults (~2–3 weeks egg-to-adult in summer).

stageBreakdown.Larvae: Spiny, black alligator-like larvae with prominent bright orange stripes along both sides.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 6–10 mm broadly oval dome-shaped beetle (colour variable) marked by a clear black 'M' or 'W' on the pale pronotum.

conditions: Active 14–30°C (best ~25–30°C) at ~70% RH.
damage: Ecological & Wine Taint Risk: Displaces native coccinellids through intraguild predation, pinches/bites humans, secretes yellow defensive haemolymph indoors, and ruins wine batches via ladybird taint if harvested inside grape clusters.
usage: Do NOT purchase or intentionally release. Monitor vineyard clusters carefully near harvest and exclude overwintering adults from homes and greenhouses.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM; Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert)

origin: Native to Australia; introduced worldwide and widely used in Canadian greenhouses, citrus, vineyards, and interiorscapes for mealybug hotspots.
crops: Citrus, Vineyards, Grapes, Ornamentals, Rose, Gerbera, Ficus, Palms, Orchids, Greenhouse crops
effects: Premier hotspot predator of mealybugs: both adults and large wax-covered larvae consume hundreds of mealybug eggs, crawlers, nymphs, and adults, and also feed on soft scales.
targets: Mealybugs (Citrus mealybug Planococcus citri, Vine mealybug Planococcus ficus, Long-tailed mealybug) and some soft scales.
appearance: Adult ~4 mm long; dark brown/black body with reddish/orange-brown head, pronotum, and posterior wing tips. Larva (up to 13 mm) is covered in long white waxy filaments, closely resembling a large mealybug ('wolf in sheep's clothing').
lifeCycle: Pre-oviposition (~3 d) -> yellow egg laid in mealybug ovisac (~5 d) -> 4 waxy predatory larval instars (~14 d) -> pupa (~7 d) -> predatory adult; total cycle ~3–5 weeks (~29 d at 25°C and 60% RH). Both larvae and adults are voracious predators.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Yellow oval eggs laid directly inside cottony mealybug egg masses (ovisacs, ~5 d).
stageBreakdown.Waxy Larvae (4 Instars): Up to 13 mm long, covered in long white wax filaments mimicking a giant mealybug (~14 d; move much faster and have visible jaws when flipped).
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~4 mm dark brown/black beetle with orange-brown head, thorax, and wing tips.

conditions: Active 16–33°C (best 25–28°C); activity stops <9°C and searching declines >33°C.
usage: Release adults or larvae directly into moderate-to-heavy mealybug hotspots (combine with Leptomastix dactylopii or Anagyrus vladimiri for low-density long-term suppression); train scouts to tell fast waxy Cryptolaemus larvae apart from true mealybugs.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

synonyms: Rhyzobius lophanthae, Scale destroyer, Purple scale predator
origin: Australian native scale-feeding lady beetle introduced to North America and used in orchards, citrus, and greenhouse ornamentals.
crops: Citrus, Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Ornamentals, Palms, Ferns, Greenhouse crops
effects: Specialist armoured and soft scale predator: strong mandibles allow both adults and hairy dark larvae to chew right through tough waxy scale shields to consume females and eggs beneath.
targets: Armoured scales (Diaspididae) and soft scales (Coccidae); also preys on mealybugs, pest mites, and caterpillar eggs.
appearance: Small (2–3 mm) shiny black, finely hairy lady beetle with a reddish-orange head and thorax (pronotum). Larva (~3.5 mm) is dark grey-brown and hairy (lacking the long white wax filaments of Cryptolaemus).
lifeCycle: Egg laid under scale cover -> 4 predatory larval instars (~3 wk) -> pupa -> adult; ~1 month (30 d) egg-to-adult at 25°C. Both adults and larvae chew through scale covers to consume scales and eggs.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Minute elongate yellow eggs tucked beneath empty or live scale covers.
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): ~3.5 mm dark grey-brown spiny/hairy larvae lacking white wax filaments (~3 wk).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm finely hairy shiny-black dome beetle with orange-red head and thorax.

conditions: Active even at cool temperatures around 5°C; best 20–30°C and >60% RH preferred. Works synergistically with scale parasitoids such as Aphytis melinus.
usage: Release onto infested trunks, palms, citrus, ferns, and woody ornamentals where scale covers show ragged chewing holes (combine with Aphytis melinus parasitoids and ant exclusion).
references: UC IPM; Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Palearctic/Holarctic specialist spider-mite-feeding lady beetle; widely used in Canadian greenhouses, hop yards, and orchards.
crops: Sweet pepper, Cucumber, Tomato, Hop, Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Berries, Ornamentals
effects: Flying hotspot specialist against dense, webbed spider mite outbreaks: adults fly accurately toward mite volatiles and consume 40–75+ mites/day while spiny dark larvae clear infested leaves even in dry air.
targets: Spider mites, especially Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), Carmine spider mite (T. cinnabarinus), European red mite (Panonychus ulmi), and Spruce spider mite (Oligonychus ununguis).
appearance: Very small (~1–1.5 mm) oval, shiny black, finely pubescent lady beetle; larva is dark gray-brown to blackish, elongated (~2–2.5 mm), and bristly.
lifeCycle: Oval pale egg (3–5 d) -> 4 predatory larval instars (~8–9 d) -> black bristly pupa on leaf (6–8 d) -> adult; total egg-to-adult ~2 weeks (14–16 d) at 26°C. Both larvae and flying adults actively locate and consume all stages of spider mites.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Minute pale oval eggs tucked flat among spider mite webbing (3–5 d).
stageBreakdown.Larvae (4 Instars): ~2–2.5 mm dark charcoal-grey bristly elongated larvae draining all mite stages (~8–9 d).
stageBreakdown.Pupae & Adults: Dark hairy pupa glued to leaf -> ~1–1.5 mm black flying coccinellid.

conditions: Active ~14–35°C (best 23–25°C; good greenhouse performance 20–30°C) and 30–90% RH (tolerates relatively dry conditions where predatory mites struggle).
usage: Deploy into heavy webbed spider mite hotspots in tomato, pepper, cucumber, hops, and orchards alongside Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus fallacis.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

synonyms: Atheta coriaria, Dalotia (Atheta) coriaria, Greenhouse rove beetle
origin: Cosmopolitan soil-dwelling rove beetle; major commercial biological control agent in Canada for greenhouse substrates, propagation media, and mushroom production.
crops: Greenhouse crops, Ornamentals, Vegetables, Seedlings, Cuttings, Herbs, Mushrooms
effects: Fast-running and strong-flying soil predator whose adults and larvae patrol rockwool, coco coir, peat, and propagation benches hunting fungus gnat larvae, shore fly maggots, soil-dwelling thrips pupae, and root mealybugs.
targets: Fungus gnat eggs and larvae (Bradysia impatiens, Lycoriella spp.), Shore fly eggs and larvae (Scatella tenuicosta), Thrips larvae/pre-pupae/pupae in substrate (Frankliniella occidentalis), springtails, and root mealybugs.
appearance: Small (3–4 mm), slender light-to-dark brown beetle with very short wing covers (elytra) leaving most of the flexible abdomen exposed; characteristically curves its abdomen upward like a scorpion when disturbed. Larvae are elongate, cream-yellow to brownish with well-developed legs.
lifeCycle: Egg in substrate (hatches in 2–3 d) -> 3 predatory larval instars (~7 d) -> pupa in soil cell (~4 d) -> winged adult (lives up to ~3 wk); total egg-to-adult ~13–14 days at 25°C. Both larvae and adults are aggressive predators; adults run fast and fly to colonize entire greenhouses rapidly.

stageBreakdown.Eggs: Microscopic oval eggs laid directly in damp growing media or substrate crevices (2–3 d).
stageBreakdown.Larvae (3 Instars): Slender pale cream-to-amber leggy soil larvae hunting fungus gnat maggots (~7 d).
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3–4 mm glossy dark-brown rove beetle with short elytra and scorpion-like upturned abdomen.

conditions: Best 20–25°C (active ~12–32°C) and 50–80% RH; moist growing medium favors establishment.
usage: Maintain permanent breeder buckets (bran/vermiculite + feed) in propagation and greenhouse bays, or sprinkle directly onto moist substrates alongside Gaeolaelaps gillespiei and Steinernema feltiae.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Biobest; Anatis Bioprotection; Koppert Biological Systems

metabolite: Hydrotaea aenescens (Black Dump Fly / Housefly Predator)
synonyms: Ophyra aenescens, Black dump fly, Housefly predator
origin: Used commercially in livestock facilities, poultry houses, dairy barns, and compost/manure management.
crops: Livestock facilities, Manure & Compost substrates
effects: Manure-dwelling predator whose 2nd and 3rd instar maggots kill 15–20 pest housefly or lesser housefly larvae per day while adults stay close to low manure pits rather than dispersing into upper structures.
targets: House fly (Musca domestica) and lesser house fly (Fannia canicularis) larvae/maggots.
appearance: Adult ~4–7 mm shiny black/blue-bronze fly with reddish eyes; larvae are slender cream-colored predatory maggots.
lifeCycle: Egg -> 3 larval instars (2nd and 3rd instars are voracious predators, each killing 15–20 housefly maggots/day) -> pupa -> adult; ~14–18 days under warm favourable conditions.

stageBreakdown.Eggs & L1: Eggs hatch inside damp organic/manure pits; 1st instars develop rapidly before switching to predation.
stageBreakdown.Predatory Maggots (L2–L3): Each L2/L3 larva kills 15–20 housefly maggots/day.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 4–7 mm glossy blue-black dump fly remaining near floor manure zones.

conditions: Best 20–30°C (efficacy reduced <15°C and >38°C) in moist/semi-liquid manure or organic substrate.
usage: Apply in poultry barns, livestock stalls, and enclosed composting zones paired with pupal parasitoid wasps (Muscidifurax raptorellus) for full maggot-plus-pupal fly suppression.

origin: Mediterranean/Old World whitefly parasitoid; less prominent in current Canadian commercial programs than Eretmocerus eremicus.
crops: Cucumber, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Poinsettia, Warm protected crops
effects: Heat-tolerant specialist parasitoid of Bemisia tabaci (Tobacco/Silverleaf whitefly): oviposits beneath young nymphs, waits until L4 to penetrate, and kills extra nymphs via host feeding.
targets: Primarily Tobacco/Silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
appearance: Tiny (~1 mm) pale lemon-yellow aphelinid wasp.
lifeCycle: Egg laid beneath whitefly nymph -> hatching larva waits/penetrates L4 host -> internal development -> pupa -> adult; also performs host feeding.

stageBreakdown.Eggs & Internal Larva: Egg placed under L2/L3 nymph; wasp larva penetrates L4 host internally.
stageBreakdown.Parasitized Pupa: Whitefly scale swells with amber/yellowish wasp pupa visible inside (does NOT turn black).
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~1 mm pale lemon-yellow wasp emerging via a round dorsal exit hole.

conditions: Active 20–32°C (best ~25–30°C); highly heat-tolerant.
usage: Effective in hot protected crops heavily infested by Bemisia tabaci; in Canadian greenhouses, Eretmocerus eremicus is more widely stocked.
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Koppert Biological Systems; Biobest

origin: Solitary endoparasitoid of mealybugs; current commercial biological control agent in Canada.
crops: Vineyards, Grapes, Citrus, Ornamentals, Rose, Greenhouse crops, Nurseries
effects: Rapidly reproducing solitary endoparasitoid against citrus and vine mealybugs: actively searches across concealed leaf axils and bark, lays eggs in nymphs/adults, and kills young nymphs via host feeding.
targets: Citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri) and Vine mealybug (Planococcus ficus).
appearance: Sexually dimorphic: female ~1.5–2 mm, brown to orange-brown with distinctive black-and-white banded antennae; male smaller (~0.8 mm), black with feathered antennae.
lifeCycle: Oviposition into mealybug nymph/adult -> egg incubation (1–2 d) -> 5 internal larval instars (5–9 d; mummification occurs at 5th instar) -> pupal stage inside cylindrical brown mummy (4–5 d) -> adult emerges (~12–16 days total at 25°C). Adult females also kill young nymphs via host feeding.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Mummy: Host turns into a hardened cylindrical brown mummy containing the pupating wasp (4–5 d).
stageBreakdown.Females: 1.5–2 mm orange-brown wasp with conspicuous black-and-white banded antennae.
stageBreakdown.Males: ~0.8 mm sleek black wasp with feathered antennae.

conditions: Active across a wide temperature range: 13–38°C (optimum ~25°C).
usage: Primary commercial encyrtid parasitoid in Canada for low-to-moderate Planococcus citri and Planococcus ficus infestations; pair with Cryptolaemus montrouzieri in hotspots.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; Koppert Biological Systems; UC IPM

synonyms: Related species: Leptomastix epona (European commercial), Leptomastidea abnormis (formerly Leptomastix abnormis)
origin: Originates from South America; widely used specialist parasitoid of Planococcus citri alongside Cryptolaemus montrouzieri.
crops: Citrus, Ornamentals, Ficus, Palms, Greenhouse crops
effects: Specialist citrus mealybug parasitoid that drums L3/L4 nymphs and young adult females with its extra-long antennae before parasitizing them internally (~18–25 days at 25°C).
targets: Citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri — prefers L3/L4 nymphs and young adult females). Does NOT effectively control long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus).
appearance: Small (2–3 mm) yellowish-brown wasp with dark brown eyes and very long dark antennae almost the length of its body (held upright and tapped on the leaf while walking).
lifeCycle: Solitary endoparasitoid: lays 1 egg per host -> larva develops inside mealybug, turning it into a legless, barrel-shaped brownish-yellow mummy covered in fine silk threads -> adult chews a round cap exit hole at one end (~18–25 days at 25°C).

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Mummy: Legless, barrel-shaped brownish-yellow mummy wrapped in fine silk threads; opened via a round exit cap at one end.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm yellow-brown wasp with dark eyes and very long upright dark antennae tapped continuously while walking.

conditions: Requires warm conditions: >=19°C (best ~25–30°C) and ~60–65% RH.
usage: Confirm species ID as Citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri) before release; combine with Anagyrus vladimiri (broad temperature span) and Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (hotspots).
references: Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert); Biobest; Koppert Biological Systems

metabolite: Aphytis melinus (Golden Chalcid / Armoured Scale Parasitoid)
synonyms: Golden chalcid, Related soft-scale parasitoid: Metaphycus helvolus
origin: Native to India/Pakistan; introduced to North America for classical and augmentative biological control of armoured scales.
crops: Citrus, Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Olives, Ornamentals, Palms, Greenhouse crops
effects: Specialist armoured-scale ectoparasitoid: female slips her ovipositor beneath the waxy scale cover to lay an egg directly on the scale body underneath, and kills additional scales via host feeding.
targets: Armoured scales (Diaspididae), especially California red scale (Aonidiella aurantii) and Oleander scale (Aspidiotus nerii), with partial suppression of San José scale (Comstockaspis perniciosa).
appearance: Tiny (~1 mm) lemon-yellow wasp with green compound eyes and 3 red ocelli.
lifeCycle: Female pierces scale cover and lays egg on the scale body underneath -> ectoparasitic larva feeds externally on the scale beneath its shield -> yellow-brown pupa forms under the scale cover -> adult chews a characteristic round emergence hole through the scale shield (~12–16 days at 25°C). Females also kill many scales by host feeding.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Scale Shield: Waxy armoured scale cover reveals a single clean, round wasp exit hole on top.
stageBreakdown.Larva & Pupa: External white-to-yellowish larva feeding beneath the shield -> yellow-brown pupa.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~1 mm bright lemon-yellow wasp with green eyes and 3 red ocelli.

conditions: Active 13–38°C (best ~25°C). Combines effectively with the scale-predatory lady beetle Lindorus lophanthae.
usage: Release during peak 2nd- and 3rd-instar virgin female scale availability and pair with Lindorus lophanthae; control ants around palms and citrus so honeydew-tending ants do not chase wasps away.
references: UC IPM; Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection

metabolite: Trichogramma brassicae (Moth Egg Parasitoid & Species Guide)
taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Trichogrammatidae (Lepidopteran Egg Parasitoid)
origin: Current Canadian commercial egg parasitoid species suited to low- and mid-canopy vegetable and field crops.
crops: Brassica, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Onions, Leek, Garlic, Sweet Corn, Corn, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Vegetables, Field crops
effects: Tiny egg parasitoid that intercepts Lepidoptera pests BEFORE caterpillars ever hatch: female inspects moth eggs, drills into fresh chorions, and kills host embryos cleanly (~7–10 days egg-to-adult at 25–30°C).
targets: Lepidoptera (moth and butterfly) eggs: Cabbage looper (Trichoplusia ni), Diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella), Leek moth (Acrolepiopsis assectella), Bertha/Cabbage armyworm (Mamestra spp.), European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), and cutworms.
appearance: Minute (<1 mm; ~0.3–0.8 mm) yellow-brown wasp with red eyes. Parasitized moth eggs turn dark charcoal-black after ~3–4 days.
lifeCycle: Female lays egg inside fresh moth host egg -> egg (1–2 d) -> internal larva consumes host embryo (3–4 d; host egg turns black) -> pupa inside host chorion (3–4 d) -> adult wasp chews exit hole (~7–10 days total at 25–30°C). Females lay ~50–80 eggs in their lifetime.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Host Egg: Healthy pale/yellow moth egg turns solid dark charcoal-black 3–4 days after parasitization (diagnostic field sign!).
stageBreakdown.Adults: Minute (<0.8 mm) yellow-brown wasp with bright red eyes.

conditions: Best 25–30°C and 60–80% RH.

usage: Hang weather-protected release cards in shade right at first adult moth trap captures; staggered multi-wave emergence inside capsules/cards covers overlapping moth egg-laying windows.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; Koppert Biological Systems; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM

origin: Eastern/central North American native egg parasitoid commercialized in Canada and the US; specialized for searching upper tree and orchard canopies.
crops: Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Berries, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blueberry, Cranberry, Forests
effects: Arboreal egg parasitoid adapted to searching upper shrub and orchard tree foliage, turning codling moth, leafroller, and spruce budworm eggs charcoal-black before larvae hatch.
targets: Codling moth (Cydia pomonella), Leafrollers (Choristoneura rosaceana), Spruce budworm, Oriental fruit moth, and other tree/fruit Lepidoptera eggs.
appearance: Minute (~0.3–0.5 mm) pale yellow-brown wasp with bright red compound eyes.
lifeCycle: Egg (1–2 d) -> larva inside moth egg (3–4 d) -> pupa in blackened host egg (3–4 d) -> adult (~8–10 days at 25°C).

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Host Egg: Orchard/berry moth eggs turn dark charcoal-black prior to wasp exit.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.3–0.5 mm yellow-brown egg parasitoid with bright red eyes.

conditions: Active ~18–29°C (best 20–29°C) at 60–80% RH.
usage: Attach egg cards at chest-to-canopy height inside apple, stone fruit, and highbush berry rows synchronized with codling moth and obliquebanded leafroller pheromone flights.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM

origin: Native to China; commercialized in the US and Canada as a specialist against the European corn borer (must be released annually).
crops: Sweet Corn, Corn, Sweet pepper, Hop, Hemp, Vegetables
effects: Specialist high-searching-efficiency parasitoid of overlapping scale-like European corn borer egg masses across corn whorls, sweet pepper leaves, hemp, and hop bines.
targets: European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis) eggs and other stalk-boring Lepidoptera.
appearance: Minute (<0.5 mm) light tan wasp with red eyes and short antennae.
lifeCycle: Egg -> internal larva -> black parasitized moth egg -> pupa -> adult (~7–9 days at 28°C).

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Egg Mass: Overlapping corn borer egg masses turn jet-black instead of hatching black-headed larvae.
stageBreakdown.Adults: <0.5 mm light tan wasp active in tall summer canopies.

conditions: Best ~28–33°C and 60–80% RH.
usage: Release annually at the first generation of European corn borer moth flight in sweet corn, pepper, hop, and hemp.
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems

synonyms: Related species: Trichogramma sibericum (studied on cabbage looper in Canada), Trichogramma evanescens (European commercial)
origin: Wide-ranging New World generalist egg parasitoid commercialized in Canada and the US.
crops: Tomato, Sweet pepper, Brassica, Cabbage, Cranberry, Berries, Corn, Vegetables, Ornamentals
effects: Versatile low-to-mid-canopy generalist moth-egg parasitoid widely deployed in tomatoes, sweet peppers, cranberries, brassicas, and ornamentals (~10 host eggs parasitized/female/day).
targets: Cabbage looper (Trichoplusia ni), Tomato hornworm, Corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea), Armyworms, Cranberry fruitworm, and many other Lepidoptera eggs.
appearance: Minute (~0.3 mm) pale yellow wasp with red eyes.
lifeCycle: Egg -> internal larva -> pupa in blackened host egg -> adult (~8–10 days at 25°C). Female can parasitize up to ~10 moth eggs/day.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Host Egg: Looped/spherical moth eggs turn black by day 3–4.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.3 mm pale yellow parasitoid active across vegetable and berry foliage.

conditions: Active 15–30°C (best ~20–25°C) at ~60% RH.
usage: Combine preventive T. pretiosum releases with Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Cotesia marginiventris in fruiting solanaceous crops and cranberry bogs.
references: Koppert Biological Systems; Anatis Bioprotection; UC IPM

origin: Western North American native (west of the Rocky Mountains, including BC and California) adapted to tree crops, orchards, and vineyards.
crops: Apple, Fruit trees, Orchards, Vineyards, Grapes, Berries, Walnuts, Avocados
effects: Western arboreal counterpart to T. minutum: tolerates warmer, drier western summer orchards and vineyards to parasitize codling moth, leafroller, and fruitworm eggs.
targets: Codling moth (Cydia pomonella), Obliquebanded and omnivorous leafrollers, Fruitworms, Twig borers, and other orchard Lepidoptera eggs.
appearance: Minute (~0.4 mm) yellow-brown wasp morphologically nearly identical to T. minutum.
lifeCycle: Develops inside moth eggs (~8–10 days at 25–28°C), turning parasitized eggs black.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Host Egg: Orchard/vineyard moth eggs blacken internally within ~4 days.
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~0.4 mm western tree-canopy wasp well adapted to Pacific Northwest summer heat.

conditions: Best 27–32°C (active 18–32°C) and 60–80% RH.
usage: Use west of the Rockies (BC Okanagan/Fraser Valley, Washington, California) in apple orchards and vineyards timed with degree-day codling moth models.
references: UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Anatis Bioprotection

metabolite: Cotesia marginiventris (and Cotesia Caterpillar Parasitoid Guide)
taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Microgastrinae
origin: Native Americas solitary koinobiont endoparasitoid of young noctuid caterpillars; CFIA-approved for biological control in Canada.
crops: Vegetables, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Brassica, Cabbage, Sweet Corn, Corn, Soybeans, Alfalfa, Field crops
effects: Solitary koinobiont endoparasitoid that targets young (1st–2nd instar) armyworms, loopers, and earworms: parasitized caterpillars stop feeding early and perish as the wasp exits to spin a clean white silken cocoon (~11–15 days at 25°C).
targets: Young (1st–2nd instar) noctuid caterpillars: Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda), Beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua), Cabbage looper (Trichoplusia ni), and Corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea).
appearance: Small (~3 mm) black braconid wasp with long antennae and a short ovipositor; mature larva spins a white silken cocoon (~4 mm) on foliage beside the dead host.
lifeCycle: Solitary koinobiont endoparasitoid: female lays egg inside 1st–2nd instar caterpillar -> host remains alive and feeds briefly while larva develops through 3 instars (~7–10 d) -> mature larva exits host and spins a white silken cocoon -> pupates inside cocoon (~3–5 d) -> adult wasp emerges (~11–15 days total at 25°C).

stageBreakdown.Parasitized L1–L2 Caterpillar: Young caterpillar feeds noticeably less and becomes sluggish before the wasp larva emerges.
stageBreakdown.Solitary White Cocoon: ~4 mm fuzzy white silken cocoon beside the shriveled caterpillar (~3–5 d pupation).
stageBreakdown.Adults: ~3 mm black braconid wasp with long antennae and short ovipositor.

conditions: Best ~22–25°C and ~65–70% RH.

usage: Release promptly when young L1–L2 loopers or armyworms hatch (pair with Trichogramma egg parasitoids and avoid mistaking white Cotesia cocoons for pest eggs).
references: Anatis Bioprotection; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Koppert Biological Systems; UC IPM

taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Microgastrinae
origin: Specialist solitary endoparasitoid of diamondback moth larvae; CFIA-approved in Canada.
crops: Brassica, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Brussel Sprout, Bok Choi, Canola, Radishes, Turnip
effects: Solitary koinobiont specialist against diamondback moth larvae: females discriminate and skip already-parasitized caterpillars, targeting L2–L3 instars cleanly inside brassica heads.
targets: Diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella) larvae.
appearance: Small (~2–3 mm) dark braconid wasp with long antennae and short ovipositor; forms a solitary white silken cocoon on brassica leaves.
lifeCycle: Solitary koinobiont endoparasitoid: parasitizes L2–L3 diamondback moth larvae (discriminates and avoids already-parasitized hosts) -> 3 larval instars inside living caterpillar -> spins solitary white cocoon -> adult emerges (~11–14 days at 25°C).

stageBreakdown.Solitary White Cocoon: ~4 mm silky white cocoon spun directly on brassica leaf surfaces.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 2–3 mm black braconid wasp with long searching antennae.

conditions: Best ~24–25°C and ~60–70% RH.
usage: Deploy alongside Trichogramma brassicae in cabbage, kale, broccoli, and Asian greens; selective biopesticides (Bt) preserve Cotesia cocoons while suppressing large instars.
references: BC Ministry of Agriculture; Anatis Bioprotection; Koppert Biological Systems

synonyms: Apanteles glomeratus, Related species: Cotesia flavipes (Stem borer parasitoid, CFIA-approved), Cotesia melanoscelus (Spongy moth parasitoid, CFIA-approved)
taxonomy: Order Hymenoptera • Family Braconidae • Subfamily Microgastrinae
origin: Introduced to North America for classical biological control of imported cabbageworm and now widely established across Canada and the US (related CFIA-approved species include Cotesia flavipes for corn/sugarcane stem borers and Cotesia melanoscelus for spongy moth Lymantria dispar in deciduous trees).
crops: Brassica, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussel Sprout, Corn, Deciduous trees
effects: Gregarious koinobiont parasitoid depositing 15–50 eggs inside young Pieris cabbageworms; mature larvae erupt simultaneously to spin bright sulphur-yellow cocoons.
targets: Imported cabbageworm (Pieris rapae) and Large white butterfly (Pieris brassicae) larvae; C. flavipes targets stem borers (Diatraea, Chilo); C. melanoscelus targets spongy moth (Lymantria dispar).
appearance: Small (~3–7 mm) dark braconid wasp with yellow-brown legs and long curved antennae. Diagnostic field sign: a cluster of 15–50 bright sulphur-yellow silken cocoons spun on or next to the dying cabbageworm caterpillar.
lifeCycle: Gregarious koinobiont endoparasitoid: female deposits 15–50 eggs into a young Pieris caterpillar -> larvae develop together through 3 instars -> mature larvae erupt simultaneously through the host cuticle and spin a tight cluster of yellow silken cocoons (~7–10 d larval dev, ~3–5 d pupation; ~15–20 d total at 25°C).

stageBreakdown.Yellow Cocoon Cluster: Unmistakable cluster of 15–50 bright sulphur-yellow oval silken cocoons atop/beside dying cabbageworm (~3–5 d pupation). NEVER crush!
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3–7 mm black braconid with amber legs and long curved antennae.

conditions: Active across temperate brassica growing conditions (tolerates >30–32°C).
usage: Do NOT destroy bright yellow cocoon clusters found on cabbage leaves — they are beneficial Cotesia pupae releasing the next generation of wasps!
references: UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Anatis Bioprotection

origin: Native North American ectoparasitoid wasp commercially available in Canada for greenhouse and high-tunnel solanaceous crops.
crops: Tomato, Potato, Sweet pepper, Aubergine, Solanaceous crops, Greenhouse vegetables
effects: Dual-action specialist against Bactericera cockerelli (Tomato/Potato psyllid): oviposits externally beneath 4th–5th instar nymphs while adult females also host-feed heavily on younger 1st–3rd instar nymphs.
targets: Tomato/potato psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli), vector of Zebra Chip disease (Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum).
appearance: Tiny (0.5–2 mm) dark/black wasp with clear wings, bright yellowish legs, and clubbed antennae in females.
lifeCycle: Dual action: female lays an egg externally on the underside of a 4th or 5th instar psyllid nymph -> ectoparasitic larva feeds beneath the nymph, turning it into a flattened copper-brown mummy anchored to the leaf -> pupates beneath mummy -> adult chews round dorsal exit hole (~12 days egg-to-adult at 26°C). Adult females also kill large numbers of younger (1st–3rd instar) psyllid nymphs via HOST FEEDING.

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Psyllid Mummy: Flattened oval scale-like psyllid nymph turns copper-brown and develops a single round dorsal exit hole.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 0.5–2 mm shiny black wasp with bright yellowish legs and clear wings.

conditions: Optimal 20–24°C (activity declines <15°C) at ~70% RH.
usage: Release weekly in greenhouse tomato, pepper, aubergine, and seed-potato structures at first sign of psyllid adults or white 'psyllid sugar' pellets, and pair with Dicyphus hesperus.
references: Koppert Biological Systems; BC Ministry of Agriculture; UC IPM

origin: Important commercial livestock-fly biological control agent currently sold in Canada.
crops: Livestock facilities, Manure & Compost substrates
effects: Gregarious idiobiont pupal parasitoid: lays multiple eggs inside hardened filth-fly puparia, stopping adult emergence of house flies and biting stable flies without biting livestock or people.
targets: House fly (Musca domestica), Stable fly (Stomoxys calcitrans), and other filth-fly pupae.
appearance: Tiny (1–3 mm) metallic purple-black to black chalcidoid wasp with clear wings.
lifeCycle: Gregarious idiobiont ectoparasitoid: female pierces the hard fly puparium and lays up to ~8 eggs on the fly pupa inside -> larvae consume the fly pupa -> pupate inside the host puparium -> multiple adult wasps chew an exit hole and emerge (~16 days egg-to-adult under warm conditions).

stageBreakdown.Parasitized Fly Puparium: Darkened oval housefly puparium showing small round exit hole(s) instead of the large broken front cap left by emerging flies.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 1–3 mm stingless metallic black wasp crawling through dry bedding and manure edges.

conditions: Best 20–30°C (efficacy reduced <15°C and >38°C) in dry manure, bedding, and fly-pupation sites.
usage: Sprinkle parasitized pupae near dry barn walls, calf hutches, and manure margins biweekly through warm fly season; combine with Hydrotaea aenescens in wetter pits.

taxonomy: Order Diptera • Family Tachinidae (~8,500–8,600 described species worldwide)
origin: Cosmopolitan family of parasitic flies; one of the most important natural biological control groups in field crops, orchards, gardens, and forests (not commercially available for augmentative release in North America).
crops: Vegetables, Brassica, Corn, Apple, Orchards, Berries, Field crops, Forests, Ornamentals
effects: Key natural biological control parasitoids suppressing agricultural caterpillars, Japanese/Colorado potato beetle grubs, stink bugs, and squash bugs; internal maggots breathe through a respiratory funnel before exiting to pupate in soil.
targets: Mostly caterpillars (armyworms, cutworms, loopers, tent caterpillars, spongy moth) and beetle larvae (Japanese beetle, Colorado potato beetle), plus true bugs (stink bugs, squash bugs), grasshoppers, and sawflies.
appearance: Adults are 3–14+ mm robust, fast-flying flies, usually gray, black, or striped and distinctly very bristly (stout bristles on the abdomen). Conspicuous white oval macrotype eggs are often visible glued directly behind the head of parasitized caterpillars.
lifeCycle: Female glues macrotype eggs onto host cuticle, deposits microtype eggs on foliage to be eaten, or larviposits live maggots -> egg incubation (~1–3 d) -> internal larval development through 3 instars (L1, L2, L3 over ~4–10 d, breathing via a respiratory funnel before consuming vital organs) -> mature maggot exits dying host -> dark reddish-brown oblong puparium in soil (~7–14 d) -> adult fly (lifespan ~1–4 weeks).

stageBreakdown.Macrotype Eggs: Conspicuous flat white oval eggs cemented right behind a caterpillar's or stink bug's head where the host cannot chew them off.
stageBreakdown.Internal Maggots (L1–L3): Develop 4–10 d inside the living host breathing via a funnel; exit dying host to drop to soil.
stageBreakdown.Adults: 3–14+ mm fast, very bristly grey/black/striped flies (distinctly more bristly on the abdomen than house flies).

conditions: Species-specific thermal and moisture requirements across temperate field, orchard, and forest habitats; adults feed on nectar and honeydew from umbelliferous and composite flowers (e.g., Yarrow, Dill, Parsley, Sweet Alyssum).
usage: Conserve natural populations by planting open nectar-producing flowers (Yarrow, Dill, Sweet Alyssum) along orchard/vegetable borders and leaving parasitized caterpillars carrying bright white eggs behind the head untreated.
references: UC IPM; BC Ministry of Agriculture; Knowing and Recognizing (Koppert)

origin: First observed on whitefly in 1915 and used commercially for biological control of whitefly since 1980; widespread across temperate, subtropical, and tropical regions.
crops: Cucumber, Tomato, Sweet pepper, Rose, Gerbera, Chrysanthemum, Ornamentals
effects: Contact fungal entomopathogen: spores germinate on the insect exterior (feeding on honeydew or penetrating the epidermis directly via germ tubes). Internal hyphal growth kills the insect through mechanical obstruction of respiratory tubes, exhaustion of energy reserves, organ disruption, and fungal proteins.
targets: Whitefly larvae (and pupae/adults at high RH; eggs are not affected) and Thrips larvae.
appearance: Dead whitefly larvae and pupae appear light to dark brown, sunken, and lose their normal sheen before white, cottony aerial hyphae (branched almost perpendicularly under a microscope) emerge through the cuticle to produce new spores. First symptoms appear in 7–10 days; full control visible 2 weeks after spraying.
lifeCycle: Produces sticky conidiospores coated in slime that are NOT airborne; dispersed via water splash, mechanical contact, or infected insects.
conditions: Requires temperatures of 15–28°C (harmed above 32°C) and relative humidity >= 80% in the leaf underside boundary layer.
usage: Spray in the late afternoon, evening, or on cloudy days to ensure >= 80% RH in the hours following application. Thorough spray coverage of leaf undersides is mandatory because it works strictly by contact.

origin: Discovered in 1815 as the cause of white muscardine disease in silkworms; occurs worldwide with isolate-specific host ranges.
crops: Tomato, Cucumber, Sweet pepper, Strawberry, Rose, Gerbera, Ornamentals
effects: Contact fungal insecticide: vegetative conidiospores germinate on the host cuticle, penetrate via germ tubes, and grow internally, producing fungal toxins that kill the insect. Larval stages are most susceptible, especially during molting (infection is often not carried over to the next instar if molting occurs immediately after spore contact).
targets: Whiteflies (larvae), Spider mites, Thrips, Aphids, Mealybugs, Beetles, and Caterpillars.
appearance: After death, infected insects become hard and mummified, covered in white fluffy mycelial growth where new airborne and contact-dispersed conidiospores are formed.
lifeCycle: Conidiospores germinate on cuticle -> germ tube penetration -> internal hyphal proliferation & toxin release -> post-mortem external white sporulation.
conditions: Requires high relative humidity for spore germination.
usage: Apply as a high-coverage contact spray in the afternoon or evening to take advantage of rising nighttime relative humidity.
